AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I was discussing disposal of our agricultural surpluses, particularly in relation to United States policy in this matter, and had just begun to mention another mechanism which the government hopes will be of help in this direction, through the establishment of a NATO food bank. Of course at the present time this bank is nothing more than a proposal on the part of the government. Unless that proposal is accepted by the NATO members, and more particularly by the United States of America, it is not likely to be very effective for the purpose the government has in mind.
Up to the present, at least as far as I know, the United States has shown no disposition to be enthusiastic about this scheme. If the minister thinks I am being unduly pessimistic about the prospects in regard to the NATO food bank, perhaps I could quote a couple of sentences from an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 5, which is not, I must say, too optimistic about this proposal. The editorial is entitled:
What Food Bank. Where?
It begins in this way:
There is probably no law against it, but it is certainly questionable procedure to ask parliament to vote money for non-existent institutions. Yet this is what Prime Minister Diefenbaker has done in explaining a $10 million item in the supplementary estimates for the storage of flour for a North Atlantic Treaty Organization food bank.
Perhaps I made a mistake earlier when I said $10 million for wheat and flour. The editorial ends in this way:
The proposal is hard to take seriously. Is it really anything more than an effort to dispose of an embarrassing surplus? If Canada's flour cannot be sold profitably in normal markets, it would be far better to make it into bread and give it away to the world's hungry. That, at least, would give some meaning to our money.
In the same paper, the day before, Mr. Duffy, the Ottawa correspondent of that paper, had this to say:
Until there is international agreement and the food bank is established, this is merely agricultural price support smelling as sweetly by
Supply-Trade and Commerce
another name, with the cost put on the account of external affairs, instead of the Department of Agriculture.
In so far as the milk powder operation is concerned, he described it as a straight bookkeeping transaction, with the debit again being dumped into the external affairs account or, in effect, as he said:
The agriculture department has sold external affairs a lot of milk.
In view of what the Minister of Agriculture has said earlier in this session, it may not be too easy for the Department of External Affairs to dispose of that milk, in spite of an optimistic statement by the Prime Minister in the house. The Minister of Agriculture said some weeks ago that though the Canadian government offered 30 million pounds of this powder as gifts to international relief agencies in January of 1958, to date only 18 million pounds has been taken. Perhaps we should not expect too much of this NATO food bank idea as an immediate means of disposing of our agricultural surpluses, valuable as the idea is and much as we hope it may be implemented as a truly effective NATO plan.
There is another point I would like to mention, which is an important one, or should be an increasingly important one in export trade. In this connection it is not a question of competing with the United States in world markets; it is a question of one of our products trying to get into the United States market, its natural and its important market. I am referring, of course, to oil. The government, and indeed the house and country generally, have taken satisfaction over the lifting of the mandatory restrictions which were imposed by the United States government on our exports of oil to that country some time ago. It is true that, whether as a result of that lifting or for other reasons, there was a 15.6 per cent increase in our exports of oil to the United States in the last month over the preceding one; but, as the financial editor of the Montreal Gazette said on June 30-and he has written a great deal and I think with intelligence and common sense on this matter-this increase in our exports of oil to the United States did not result in any production benefit in Canada, because it was more than offset by a drop in the demand for western oil in Ontario owing to an increase in imports in that part of Canada from the United States and from Venezuela. I quote a paragraph from his article on that point. He said:
The matching of sales to the United States by American sales to Canada strengthens the suspicion that there is not, and hasn't been for some time, a "natural market" for oil and petroleum products.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Perhaps it is difficult indeed to talk realistically about a natural market for a product of this kind which is under such complicated and important international corporation control. We all hope that our exports of oil to the United States will increase. Notwithstanding the difficulties of using the term "natural market", it would seem that this part of the United States, the northwest and the west, is or should be in a rational economic world the natural market for our oil. Yet there are important incentives to United States companies to import from other sources than from their Canadian subsidiaries, and those incentives are going to make it difficult, I think, notwithstanding the removal of restrictions, to increase our exports to that country.
One difficulty is that Canadian exports of oil to the United States market are prorated over all the Canadian companies. The United States subsidiary in Canada must therefore share its export business with competing companies, but that is not the case with the United States subsidiary in other parts of the world. Second, the margin of profit to a United States company is much greater in oil from other areas than from Canada, especially, I suppose, the mid-eastern oil fields. Then there is and will be heavy political pressure on United States companies in these foreign fields, especially the Middle Eastern fields, to take the maximum amount of oil from these fields for the United States, because the more oil the United States companies take the greater the royalties will be to the local governments or rulers, and any reduction of United States imports from these fields to the advantage, if you like, of Canada would mean, and indeed has meant in the not too distant past, threats of nationalization by these local potentates.
We must remember also in connection with this oil problem that paragraph C(2) of the presidential proclamation exempting Canadian oil from quota restrictions made it perfectly clear that the quotas would be re-established if Canadian oil began to compete with United States oil through large volumes of imports. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the Calgary Herald was being quite realistic when it said in an editorial on May 4, 1959:
It is quite possible that the lilting of the United States import quotas will do Canadian independence and Canadian control of its resources a great deal of harm. . . . Keeping the trade lines flowing west to east and vice versa is Canada's age old problem. It may soon be clear that the United States import decision, which will probably bring only slight economic relief, will exact a greater price from Canadian independence.
fMr. Pearson.]

No doubt what the newspaper meant is that if because of the removal of these restrictions we assume that our oil is now going to move easily across the border into the United States and production can go up for that purpose, and we lose the interest in the eastern Canadian market that has been created in the past because of restrictions, perhaps in the long run we will suffer by this removal.
The minister is quite as aware as any member of the house that notwithstanding this action taken, by the United States government, the long range problem remains of ensuring a market for our Canadian oil to take care of increased production and that if that market, through one method or another and in spite of United States governmental action which may seem to benefit us, becomes impossible in the northwestern states or is limited to that area, one day the question of marketing that oil in eastern Canada will have to be faced seriously.
I know, as the minister knows, the difficulty that will involve, the governmental intervention and governmental interference that might involve, and I know that the lines of this trade at this time at least should be moving north and south across the border. But if that cannot be done, and if it becomes clear that even without restrictions that is not going to be done, then any government in Canada faced with that problem will have to give serious consideration to the action required to market the oil in eastern Canada.
There is one other commodity I want to mention. I have already indicated to the minister that I would be talking about it. It is the problem mentioned this morning by the hon. member for Timiskaming with respect to uranium and the development of atomic energy. I know the Canadian government has made certain bilateral agreements to facilitate and increase the marketing of this essential commodity, which has now become such an important factor in our export trade that this year the figure may reach $300 million or more. This puts it right up in the top half dozen commodities.
I believe, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, that agreements have now been reached, apart from our agreements with the United States and the United Kingdom, with Pakistan, West Germany, Japan and I think with Switzerland. If there are any additional agreements perhaps he will inform the committee. I wonder whether under these agreements, apart from the United Kingdom and the United States, any contracts have been signed for the supply of uranium itself.
I am also anxious to know-the minister mentioned this matter this morning, and gave

us some assurance in this regard-whether the stipulations we are observing because we signed a United Nations convention to this effect-and it would have been impossible for us not to have done so-in respect of guarantees for the non-military use of uranium are being observed by other exporters. I think the minister has set at rest some of the doubts we may have had from press reports on that score, but it would not be a very happy position for Canada if, having scrupulously observed the provisions of an international agreement in this regard which do bind our hands in some respects, we found that competing countries were not taking the same scrupulous attitude toward these agreements.
The other day the minister announced in the house the signing of an agreement with Japan; but that agreement, important as it may become, is not of the same type as the agreement which the United States signed with Japan a year or two ago and in which were included provisions for the actual supply of uranium. In the agreement of June, 1958 the United States makes available over a term of ten years a net amount of 2,700 kilograms of uranium 235 sold or leased to Japan for use in research and experimental work with power reactors. But I understand that our agreement with Japan is merely an enabling agreement, that there is no assurance that any uranium will be sold under that agreement, and that there are negotiations proceeding at the present time with Japan for the implementing of this agreement by an actual contract for the sale of uranium. If the minister can inform us about that matter it would be interesting information for the committee to receive.
There is no doubt, as the hon. member for Timiskaming pointed out, that we are going to be subjected to the stiffest kind of competition from the United States and perhaps also from the United Kingdom in the supply of uranium, and I am not sure that the kind of competition we are facing from the United States is equal competition any more than it has been in the case of some agricultural products.
The United States certainly have the jump on us in this matter. They made their agreement with Japan a year and a half ago; I understand they have now made 17 other bilateral agreements, and that a part of most of their agreements, which I do not think is included in our agreements, deals with the sale by the United States government on easy terms of reactors which are, as was pointed out this morning, designed to use only enriched uranium, the kind we do not produce but which is produced in the United States.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
For instance, in the agreement the United States have made with the European atomic agency, EURATOM, they have included provision for a long term loan of $135 million and a ten year guarantee with respect to the supply of enriched uranium. Therefore this is going to mean very stiff competition indeed for our uranium producers even if we are able to make agreements with all these countries.
The United Kingdom is also entering this field in a big way. The United Kingdom as I have said, has made a ten year agreement with EURATOM. I do not know whether as part of that agreement or as part of the negotiations United Kingdom reactors are to be supplied to these European countries, but I have read that the United Kingdom Dragon reactor is the choice of 12 of them. If these European countries do use that kind of reactor we may find we have again been left behind in what is becoming a highly competitive field.
I hope that will not happen as much as the minister does, but while I do not go as far as the hon. member for Timiskaming in condemning the lack of arrangements and the lack of planning in this regard, I say it would be unfortunate indeed if the Canadian type reactor, which we are led to believe is as modern, as advanced and as efficient as any in the world, is going to be pushed aside for United Kingdom and United States reactors which use enriched uranium because of financial and other advantages in the agreements made by the United Kingdom and the United States. *
It is therefore of the greatest possible importance, as was emphasized this morning, to get our CANDU reactor built soon in Canada, to show what it can do and to try to make the maximum progress possible in providing Canadian reactors and Canadian uranium in the world market. I know the minister has announced that the first Canadian power reactor should be in operation in 1964 or 1965. I know that plans have been made to that end. I should like to ask the minister whether any other provinces have shown any interest in this project and have requested reactors for power purposes, and whether the government is in touch with the provinces for the purpose of encouraging that kind of development. It certainly is necessary, as I pointed out in the beginning of my remarks, that both industry and government at the provincial and federal levels show initiative, drive and planning so we will not be left behind, not only in the international market but perhaps at home.
The importance of this matter in terms of the future was stressed by the chairman of the Ontario hydroelectric commission, Mr. HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce Duncan, in an interview on June 12, when he said that once the first big nuclear plant is built, relatively rapid progress would take place, and by 1980 about one-third of the total Ontario power production may come from nuclear energy. However, about a day later in the same newspaper there was an article by the same writer, Mr. Anderson, pointing out the fact that Canadian industry is not showing boldness, initiative and drive but is leaving too much to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. If this is related to what Mr. Duncan has said, if we are, as he has suggested to get one third of Ontario power resources from nuclear energy by 1980, then industry, according to this article, will have to show more drive and initiative than has been the case in the past.
I do not need to dwell on the importance of this matter. The minister knows its importance. It is important not only to export trade to build these reactors and develop power from atomic energy, but it is important also from the point of view of domestic development in this connection. We have a particular situation at Elliot Lake, which is the world's largest uranium producing area, I suppose, at the present time. That whole community, as the minister mentioned this morning, is uneasy about the future and has a feeling of insecurity because the contract with the United States, which takes practically all the uranium from the area, will expire in 1962.
The minister pointed out that five or six years ago it was impossible to foresee future production. But we know now that there has been a great increase in United States production of uranium. While the markets of the world around 1970 or 1972 may require all the uranium that can be produced in the world, if some steps are not taken between 1962 when this contract expires and those years when the peaceful uses of atomic energy will have developed to bridge that gap, then this community may disappear.
Elliot Lake has been constructed to last. It is a thriving, progressive community whose people have pride in it. But it might suffer to the point where it would become like the ghost towns of the thirties. This is a problem that weighs on everybody's mind in that particular community. The sooner, therefore, the government can make some announcement of the intention of the United States to renew the option which expires in 1962, the better it will be not only for that area but for our whole uranium trade.
I suggest to the minister that if the United States government is to be prevailed upon


to renew these options it will require diplomatic pressure at the highest possible level. It may even require, and perhaps it should, intervention by the Prime Minister with the President. This is a matter of major importance. I remember that a few months ago the director of the division of raw materials of the United States atomic energy commission speaking in Wyoming made a very gloomy prediction from our point of view concerning the future markets for uranium in the United States. He said at that time that it was expected the United States government's uranium procurement program would be based primarily on the utilization of its own resources.
But he also said at that time that in the latter part of 1948 they had an urgent military requirement for uranium. As one who was in the government at that time I know how urgent that requirement was. I know the pressure that was brought to bear on the Canadian government to make every possible effort to get this field going, and that was done. We were told that in doing so it was not only important from the point of view of commercial development in Canada, but it was a great service to the defence of the free world that this vital strategic material should be in abundant supply in time for the United States to build up its atomic weapons as a deterrent against war.
As I have said before in this house and perhaps I can repeat now that after having done that, after having built this community in Elliot Lake-not a community of shacks which could be torn down, with the people stealing away to find other jobs when the uranium mines were out of commission, but a community which has been carefully planned and built, that having done this and the United States now having found uranium in their own country, are they going to come to Canada and say, we now have uranium of our own; thanks very much, and good bye? This would be an intolerable situation.
I can only express the strong hope, which I am sure the minister and every member of this house shares, that the United States government will not take that position but will renew the options and thereby ensure that there will be full activity in this area from 1962 until the time comes, as it certainly will come, when this district and other uranium districts will not have to depend on atomic weapons because of the development of atomic energy for non-military purposes.
I suggest also to the minister that a very good place to locate that reactor would be in the Elliot Lake, Blind River, Thessalon

area, not only because it is suited for that purpose with a good rock foundation and an abundance of water as well as a great supply of uranium, but because in this period from 1962 to 1970, a period which may be difficult for these people, this would give them a feeling of security. The construction of this plant would help out and would help remove this fear which is hanging over them now. I am sure the minister knows all about it, because he had a visit from the chamber of commerce the other day, and I am sure they made an impression on him.
It seems to me that I have detained the committee for a long time, but I do not apologize because the matters I have brought before the committee are important. I have tried to deal with them in a constructive way, and I hope the government might give consideration to these suggestions.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the passing of the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), but at the request of farmers and grain merchants in the district of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, I want to say a few words on their behalf. It is about the grain elevator, at Sorel, where dealers in my riding are now barred from fetching their grain by truck. The elevator operators refuse to load the trucks of dealers of my district and also refuse to store their grain for domestic consumption.
Five ridings to the north of Sorel, and six to the south, have been taking their grain from the North American Elevator at Sorel for the past 40 years. As you probably know, the Sorel elevator is closest to our farms and, consequently, dealers could get their grain at much more favourable transport rates and subsidies than if they had to fetch it from other ports.
Mr. Chairman, that information has been given me by a number of dealers in my district, and more particularly by Mr. Brissette, owner of the firm J. W. Brissette Registered at St. Felix de Valois, in the riding of Joliette, who wrote to me about this.
The Sorel elevator is managed by Mr. Robert Campbell, who is also president of two important shipping firms. Last spring, he flatly refused to stock grain for the domestic market giving as a reason that he makes much more money with less trouble by stocking, loading and unloading only grain for export, which he receives from the wheat board and other Winnipeg exporters.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am asking that this gentleman, who is licensed by the wheat
Supply-Trade and Commerce board, conform to the terms of that licence.
If my information is accurate, the owner of the Sorel elevator has no right to refuse district dealers to go and fetch their grain by truck and, in addition, has to let them store their grain for local consumption.
At present, dealers in my district have to go and fetch their grain in other ports, in Montreal for instance. Transport costs are consequently much higher, and the farmers have to foot the bill.
Would the hon. minister please draw the wheat board's attention to that situation, so that this citizen of Sorel might be requested to conform to the terms of his licence, if he wants to keep it.
Therefore, this gentleman should first be asked to store enough grain for domestic consumption, and second, to allow dealers in my riding to go and fetch their grain by truck.
Those, Mr. Chairman, were the few remarks I wanted to make in the interest of the farmers and dealers in my district.

Mr. Chairman, our fisheries are one of the most important industries in the Dominion of Canada, and are contributing more and more to the wealth of our great country. The fisheries are undoubtedly one of our mainstays and one of the chief factors in the wealth of our great dominion which stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We may spend huge sums of money on mineral products and open newly discovered mines; we may spend millions on agriculture and give every assistance possible to our farmers, yet we will not have an industry any greater or more helpful to the economy of Canada than our fish industry.
It was Lord Bacon who said that the fisheries of Newfoundland alone were richer than the mines of Mexico and Peru. Every year thousands of dollars worth of codfish, herring, lobster, salmon, squid, caplin, turbot, halibut, sole, mackerel, shrimp, scallops and many other species of fish are caught. To minimize the importance of any part of the industry, or to neglect a facet or problem pertaining to any province could, in my opinion, have a drastic effect. I now refer particularly to Newfoundland and the cancellation of the NAFEL licence as of June 15, so they would no longer have the sole right to export Newfoundland salt codfish to foreign markets.
6120	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce There was no mention, or tor that matter any intimation, of concern by the government of Canada as to how this would affect the general economy of the Newfoundland fishery. There were therefore many questions left hanging unanswered with respect to this announcement, because of which there are many who are now asking these questions and are showing great concern.
Will the Newfoundland exporters be protected? Can the price level be maintained? To whom should we look for these answers? While there may have been some dissatisfaction or misunderstanding with the Newfoundland Associate Fish Exporters Limited, mainly because the organization was composed of exporters only, and though it may have been looked upon as a combine, it constituted a protection to the industry, a protection which at the present time we do not have.
A combine of any type which solely involves private enterprise is not always favoured, either at home or in the markets, and we look to the government of Canada for something to take its place. We want a control that will give protection and at the same time concern itself not only with exports but with the welfare of the industry as a whole, and of course we need a set-up that will establish better relations in our foreign markets. For ten years since confederation the life of NAFEL had been repeatedly extended while something else was being sought to take its place. The solution to this problem was always considered the prime responsibility of the government. Why all of a sudden was it dropped, leaving the industry with no protection at all?
There seems to be a tendency to overlook some of Newfoundland's problems or to treat them with a "who cares" or a "so what" attitude. The announcement of the cancellation of NAFEL came at a time when other actions concerning Newfoundland, bearing much the same stigma, were taking the limelight. NAFEL's licence has been cancelled by the government, but as far as this house or Newfoundland is concerned it has not been replaced by anything better.
In conclusion I would stress the importance of increased and concentrated effort on our behalf in research and investment in the fishery industry here in Canada. It can be concluded that a greater part of the future world economy must and will stem from the products of the sea, and there is no reason why Canada should not be prominent in such a picture. It is therefore hoped, Mr. Chairman, that those responsible will not overlook the role that Canada can and must play.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take no more than five minutes 

of the committee's time to put forward to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) a request concerning his department's general policy, which in fact has hardly changed since the Conservative party took office. Without discussing his department's general policy at any great length, I merely wish to mention a point about which many discussions took place and promises were made in the last two election campaigns. I refer to the wheat question.
I read in a paper, not so long ago, perhaps two or three weeks, that the Canadian government will have to pay $40 million in storage fees alone for Canada's surplus wheat. That is quite a contrast with all the promises we had heard in this regard.
Another point I wanted to discuss is the lack of small industries in my constituency and area. As my colleagues know, I come from Lake St. John, where tremendous water resources are being used by companies which, I must say, have been of great benefit to the area. Unfortunately, the Aluminum Company has lost a large part of its foreign markets, particularly in the United Kingdom and France and, as a result, there have been lay-offs in Arvida that are causing great hardship to the citizens of my constituency and to those of the neighbouring constituency of Chicoutimi.
The same thing happened to the Price Brothers company, which operates two mills, one at Jonquiere and the other at Kenogami, in my riding. Many workers at the Price Brothers mills are now putting in only 28, 30 or 32 hours a week. I am sure it is no fault of the company because, there again, foreign markets play their part and heaven knows that Price Brothers have a very long and creditable record in the development of natural resources in the Saguenay-Lake St. John district.
Here is what I should like to ask the minister: about six or eight weeks ago, the mayors of municipalities in the four constituencies of our area came here to meet the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). The Minister of Labour, after having considered the brief submitted by the committee of our district, did not hesitate to tell us, in all frankness, that what we needed most was small industry. We have aluminum and pulpwood, but if foreign markets fall off, and men are laid off, hardship results.

I am not trying to play politics with this, Mr. Chairman, but I say that my constituency, at the present time, is one of the hardest hit by unemployment. That is why I ask the minister whether it would not be possible next fall, to send out into our area some experts from the federal Department of Trade and Commerce, perhaps from the division of industrial development, to consider the possibility of developing some use for by-products of our aluminum or pulp-wood.
I know that the aluminum company itself has done research in that direction but, on the other hand, I also know that the chief concern of the aluminum company is to market its own products.
It seems to me that our people, municipal authorities in Chicoutimi, Jonquiere, Arvida and Kenogami, should set up a bureau, some sort of industrial development office which, with the help of federal government experts, could perhaps find ways to help us set up small industries that would absorb some of the men who were laid off because of declining world markets.
I therefore ask the minister to be kind enough to say a few words on this matter when he replies to the other members who expressed their views on the first item.
