I was interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming this morning. As my leader has pointed out, the leading demand for uranium in the future will be through its purchase for use in reactors for the production of electric power. The industries of Europe are power hungry, and as they expand they will have to rely on other sources of power. Just as coal is giving place to oil, I think in the future we can look forward to a time when oil itself will be displaced by electrical energy produced from nuclear reactors.
Both the United Kingdom and the United States have pioneered the development of reactors for this purpose, the United States using one kind of uranium and the United Kingdom using another. The United States has already taken steps by an aggressive trade policy to safeguard her position in the world market and, possibly, to secure control of it. The competition, therefore, is between the United States and the United Kingdom, and it will be a competition between the pocket-
Supply-Trade and Commerce book of the United States treasury and the skill and experience of United Kingdom scientists and engineers, who will have to offset their dollar disadvantage by increased efficiency in their plants and by reduced costs of production and operation.
It seems to me that here is an opportunity for Canada to assist the United Kingdom and to help herself at the same time. I have been told that one of the problems with regard to producing uranium is the disposal of the heat generated in the process and, as the hon. member for Timiskaming has pointed out, at Hamilton falls in Labrador we not only have an abundance of energy but we also have cold water, a refrigerant which would take care of the heat problem. I do not pretend to know enough about the economics of the industry to be able to say whether it is cheaper to bring the Hamilton falls power to the ore or carry the ore to the power, or whether the advantage of having this cold water is enough to offset the shipping costs, but it seems to me we should try to overcome these difficulties and arrange an agreement in co-operation with the United Kingdom by means of which we could help Britain to meet the competition from the United States. By doing so we should be not only improving the position of the United Kingdom but advancing and safeguarding our own interests as well.
My real reason for rising at this time is to ask the minister whether any effort has been made by Canadian companies with or without federal assistance, to establish flour mills in Nigeria. Nigeria is a large country with a population of 50 million people, three times that of Canada, and next year she is going to have an independent government and will become one of the leading nations of Africa. I am told that the Nigerians consume a considerable quantity of flour which is milled in the United States. It seems to me that we should try to have Canadian mills established in Nigeria so we can ship over the wheat and they can take advantage of their low labour costs to supply themselves with food at a fairly cheap price. I am sure if we do not take this step the United States will. In my opinion this is the kind of action we should be taking in these new countries to ensure future markets to take care of our surpluses.
I would hope that something like this could be done not only with respect to surplus wheat but with respect to surplus fish. In Newfoundland at this time of year we produce a large surplus of small trap fish a great deal of which cannot be economically processed either by salting or by freezing. I should like to see the Department of Trade

Supply-Trade and Commerce and Commerce get together with the Department of Fisheries to see if some way cannot be worked out to can this fish so it could be made available to countries like Nigeria and other African countries at a price which they could afford and which would not require them to go to the expense of setting up expensive refrigeration facilities. I am sure if we can do something like that we will not only be securing markets for future surpluses, but we will be putting our surpluses to a good ideological use.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to say a word or two in support of the representations that have been made to the Ontario hydroelectric power commission and to the minister in connection with the possible location of the nuclear power plant in the Sturgeon Falls area. I recognize that on this point I have a friendly difference of opinion with my leader.
I urge the minister to pay no attention to the hon. member.
That lets me out.

However, I am sure the minister will be able to give my request appropriate consideration. This is the first opportunity I have had to mention this to the minister.
I received communications only yesterday to substantiate the representations that have been made over the past year by the municipality.
I quite recognize the role the Ontario hydroelectric power commission plays in the choice of these sites and I would point out that on August 7, 1958 the town of Sturgeon Falls wrote the commission requesting that consideration be given to that town as a possible site for Ontario's first full scale nuclear power plant. On August 10 there was an acknowledgement from Mr. Duncan, chairman of the board, advising the municipality that Sturgeon Falls was the first municipality in the province of Ontario to make application for this plant.
Those who are living in the district of Nipissing and particularly the people in Sturgeon Falls feel that the area is well suited as a location and is capable of taking care of this development. There are large areas of land available and all the water that is necessary. There are transportation facilities and good communications in the area. Sturgeon Falls is strategically located in northern Ontario. I would appeal to the minister at this time to give the request from the municipality of Sturgeon Falls the fullest possible consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to interpose myself between my


leader and the hon. member for Nipissing, but if the minister does have any difficulty in that regard I am sure he will recognize the value of the invitation that I now extend to him to see that this plant is situated in Essex county.
I rise at this time simply to point out something which I believe is of great importance particularly to southwestern Ontario, and as well to the agricultural community in Canada generally. I realize there is an overlapping between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce, but as this is a matter of international trade it will be of primary concern to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I believe there is some apprehension felt in Canada-and I am sure the minister is aware of this-concerning action on the part of some agricultural organizations in the United States, among them, the American farm bureau federation, and the suggestion that their representations to the government of the United States be accepted for countervailing duties against certain agricultural products from Canada. This is a matter of very great importance. When one looks at the statistics of Canadian exports of hogs and cattle, he will appreciate the significance of this trade to Canada.
For instance, I note that in 1958 Canadian exports to the United States were estimated at 62 million pounds of pork, along with 54 million pounds of beef and veal and 636,862 head of dutiable cattle. This represents a 126 per cent increase over 1957 for pork, a 13 per cent increase over 1957 for beef and veal and a 74 per cent increase over 1957 for dutiable cattle. If there were any serious interference with these exports to the United States it would be a matter of great concern for the Canadian hog producer and cattle dealer.
As the minister knows much better than I do, Canadian hog marketings have increased sharply in the last six months, and were 33 per cent greater during the first quarter of 1959 than in the same period in 1958. Whatever has been the cause of this increase, I am sure we will all recognize that the government price support program has had some effect in this situation.
We have had reverse situations in Canada with regard to United States exports of certain agricultural products during the past year. We have not taken serious retaliatory action, and it would be a matter of the greatest regret if the United States acted on the strong lobby that is now under way in that country for the imposition of countervailing duties. I merely rise to indicate what I am sure is in the minister's mind, and to

emphasize on behalf of farmers in southwestern Ontario in particular their very deep concern about the possibility of action being taken in the United States with respect to this matter.
There is just one other matter I would like to mention on these estimates, a matter I brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture the other day but which primarily concerns the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That is an interview given by the secretary of agriculture for the United States on Saturday last to Mr. Harold Morrison of the Canadian Press in Washington, when the former suggested the desirability of free trade, particularly, he said, in farm products, between the United States and Canada. He then amended his statement and said that it would also apply, of course, to trade in general.
I do not want to engage in a theoretical discussion of the desirability of free trade, but desirable as that is as an objective, I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce would agree that one would want to examine why the secretary of agriculture put forward this proposal at this time.
The other day when we were discussing the international wheat agreement, which will start to run from August 1, the minister pointed out that under the new treaty the agricultural surplus disposal policy of the United States, or of any other country, would come under annual scrutiny of the wheat council provided for under article 21 of that treaty. The minister had indicated that as a result of such scrutiny, while there would be no legal prohibition in respect of noncommercial transactions that offended certain countries in the matter of surplus farm products disposal policy, nevertheless there would be a curative effect. It might well be that this statement by the Secretary of Agriculture the other day was intended to provide another way out for the disposal of United States farm products in a manner which would be very damaging to this country.
I come, of course, from the great corn belt in Canada. The counties of Kent and Essex grow 65 per cent of the corn grown in our country. In the United States there is a surplus of 1,500 million bushels of corn, valued at $2,470 million. I associate these figures with the statement of the Secretary of Agriculture. I would hope that if we are going to consider free trade-and I hope we will-it will be done on such terms and in such a manner as not to prejudice the interests of Canadian agriculture and industry generally. The prospect this year in the United States is for a record corn crop of
Supply-Trade and Commerce 4,209 million bushels. While much of this may go for need this year, nevertheless it will present the United States with a serious problem. That will be so not only for the government of the United States. If this corn is shipped to Canada there would be the most serious consequences for the corn growers in southwest Ontario.
The same is true with regard to wheat. As of July 1 the wheat surplus in the United States I believe was 1,300 million bushels. That represents $3,500 million of the United States taxpayers' money, and I can very well understand why Mr. Benson should be anxious to find ways and means of getting rid of this surplus. If the minister feels that he has some corrective mechanism through the wheat council under the international wheat agreement, I hope he is aware, as I am sure he is, of the great dangers now implicit in this statement of the Secretary of Agriculture who undoubtedly has in mind seeking to find in Canada a market for some of this surplus corn in particular.
I would not be doing my duty even at this late date in the session if I did not raise this matter on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, together with the great concern which farmers generally have for the campaign now under way in the United States for the imposition of countervailing duties that could have such a very serious effect on Canadian hog marketings.

Madam Chairman, I also would like to say a few words on trade, but I am after some information. I would like the minister to give us an explanation, if he will, as to the policy and activities of his department in relation to the extension of Canadian trade, in particular as it relates to the United Kingdom. I ask for that information, Madam Chairman, because I find it most difficult to reconcile the statements of the minister with his actions. They seem completely contradictory in some circumstances.
I would refer the committee to the statement that was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this house on Thursday, May 28 of this year. He was making a policy statement which followed the removal of restrictions on certain United Kingdom dollar imports. The minister really waxed enthusiastic about the meaning of this to Canada and the opportunities that would be opened up for further exports of our Canadian goods. I should like to quote just two sentences of the statement made by the minister at that time. They will be found on page 4103 of Hansard, in the second column.

Supply-Trade and Commerce The minister had this to say, and he was speaking of the removal of certain restrictions in the United Kingdom:
This will open up new opportunities for the expansion of Canada's export trade, and will contribute to the desirable strengthening of trade relations between Canada and the United Kingdom.
Further on he said:
...but we hope it will not be too long before we shall see the end of the restrictions against dollar goods which the United Kingdom and other sterling area countries have felt obliged to maintain throughout the post-war period.
I think the minister made it clear as to what he felt could be the probable results of the policy actions that were taken in the United Kingdom at that time. But, as I think we all know, you cannot expect to sell goods unless you put on a selling campaign. I have always thought the minister understood that; therefore I was very surprised when, only a few days later, I read a report from one of the best-known columnists of Canada, namely Jack Scott, who is now stationed in the United Kingdom. Under date of June 6 the Sunday Sun and a great many of the papers in Canada carried a long column dealing with how this government, how Canada, has approached the opportunity of extending its sales in the United Kingdom. I would like to read the entire column. I will not take up the time of the committee doing that, but I do want to quote a couple of paragraphs. This happens to be a dispatch from London, and it says:
A pathetic little mound of packaged cheese from Ontario; a single case of canned sockeye salmon from British Columbia; and that was it.
That was the grand total of Canada's contribution to the first exhibition of commonwealth food and drinks which ended here this week and now goes on tour of the British isles, a travelling indictment of Canadian lack of initiative in seeking world markets.
If I were a Canadian in the business of selling any kind of food or drink-or, for that matter, any other exportable product with a potential market in the United Kingdom-I'd be hollering to Ottawa to demand the reason why.
More than a quarter of a million Londoners, it is estimated, have ogled and sampled the goodies from the far-flung corners of what was once the empire.
Now the display is off for Newcastle, Edinburgh, Glasgow and other points as yet undecided-"a howling success" in the words of its sponsors, the commonwealth union of trade, and all too clearly a howling flop for Canada.
Canada, in fact, was the invited guest who not only failed to show, but sent no apology.
Having regard to the statement made on the floor of the house on Thursday, May 28, and the opportunity that was opened up, even if all the restrictions were not immediately removed I think there is something wrong when we have a report from London by one of our best-known Canadian columnists who

tells us that this exhibition, the first of its kind, was completely ignored except for a pathetically small amount of packaged cheese from Ontario and a single case of sockeye salmon from British Columbia. Even if there was no market immediately available, surely having the products of Canada and the trade names of Canada on display there would have been a good start for when the remaining restrictions were removed.
I am given to understand that around this very time there was a substantial removal of restrictions. I should like to ask what is going on in the minister's department, because I am told that although the matter was put to headquarters in London the answer was that it was up to the federal government, and the federal department took no action whatsoever. All I am asking is one thing. Will the minister please explain his statement and the contradiction of no action? Will he not agree that if we want to sell we have to do a selling job, and that we cannot do it by sitting on our fannies and waiting for orders to come in automatically?
I will answer the question right now. Again here is the hon. member trying to cry down Canada and make it appear that Canada is not active and alert.
We are trying to build it, not cry it down.

We are trying to build but my hon. friend is trying to cry it down. He takes an article, and I do not care how important the correspondent is, aimed at casting a slur on Canadian businessmen and Canadian enterprise because we did not enter a food display in London. I have the article. I know the facts concerning this matter, and the article is overemphasized criticism which in my opinion was uncalled for. I am surprised at the hon. member putting the article on the record in the House of Commons, trying to make out that Canada is not alert and that the Department of Trade and Commerce has no policy with regard to trade matters.
My hon. friend reads my statement in Hansard, as found on page 4103, and he says, "There is the statement of the minister; here is the lack of action on the part of the department." He does so on the basis of one article by one correspondent with regard to a retail trade exhibition in the city of London. My hon. friend condemns the government, the department and Canada for not being alert in matters of trade when we are the fourth greatest trading nation in the world. I am surprised that my hon. friend who normally is objective in his comments, would not have seen through this article.

1 will say this to him. No information concerning this matter was forwarded to Ottawa in time for us to do anything about it. Until the import liberalizations were announced early in June by the United Kingdom government-my hon. friend recognized this fact -food products of Canadian origin could only enter the British Isles subject to quota. If you are subject to a quota there is not much incentive to advertise your products. There was a limit on the products that might go from Canada to the United Kingdom. My hon. friend, coming from British Columbia, knows what happened to the salmon catch last fall. The minute the quota was removed the catch was snapped up right away. There was certainly no need to advertise British Columbia salmon in the United Kingdom. I have been over there. I know what the people think of British Columbia salmon. It is a luxury to them, and the minute they see any British Columbia salmon it is purchased.
But now, thanks to the action of the United Kingdom authorities, the opportunity is wide open to Canadian businessmen to enter again the United Kingdom market with the food products of Canada and display their wares. It is not the sole responsibility of the government to display these wares, and I am sure that our active and alert Canadian businessmen, who have kept Canada's position as a world trader well to the fore, will be in the United Kingdom market with alacrity now that the opportunity has been opened to them.
I regret that this article should have received such prominence. I regret there should be this condemnation of Canada by a Canadian, and that it should then be elevated to the prominence which things are given by being mentioned in the House of Commons. Let me say this about the exhibition in question, an exhibition of commonwealth food and drinks. It has a good idea behind it, but it is only one of dozens of similar small shows staged annually in the United Kingdom. It is impractical for us to enter them all. We think it is much more productive for us to take part in the periodic shows sponsored by a particular trade for the benefit of the businessmen concerned rather than in exhibitions primarily attended by the public. In other words this was a retail exhibition, and now that the United Kingdom market has been reopened there is an opportunity for our Canadian food exporters and our trade representatives in Great Britain, who are very active people and who work hard to exploit new opportunities.
May I point out to my hon. friend that the department will be participating in the major United Kingdom food exhibition, the British food fair, at Olympia, London, when it takes place next year. When we come to the next
Supply-Trade and Commerce item in the estimates I can give my hon. friend and others who are interested a list of the trade fairs in which Canada is going to take part this year. It is a very important list, and shows the activity of the department and of Canadian businessmen. But for my hon. friend to take this article concerning this exhibition and the fact that there were not a large number of Canadian food products displayed there as an indication and evidence that Canada's trade policy is ineffective is, in my opinion, stretching the argument very, very far indeed.

On the same subject may I say that I do not think the minister adds to his status one bit, when he is touched a little on a sore spot, by trying to bluster his way out of it, by attacking the motives of a member of this house and by casting aspersions on the person who happened to write the article. I think I know the reason. It is simply that the person who wrote the article, Jack Scott, knew exactly what he was saying, and the proof that he was not simply engaging in wild guessing or trying to hurt Canada is the fact that identical information is on the files of the minister and is contained in an answer given by the minister in reply to a question on June 30 of this year. The questions and answers read as follows:
1.	Was the Canadian government invited to participate in a recent exhibition of commonwealth food and drinks in the United Kingdom, sponsored by the commonwealth union of trade?
2.	If so, what was the reply of the government?
Answer: No invitation was received in Ottawa.
Officials in Canada house, London, were approached about participation but declined because it is not policy to take part in shows that do not offer hope of trade promotion benefit.
In this instance, with import quotas for most Canadian foods already filled, inquiries evoked by a departmental display could not have been satisfied-and might have done more harm than good where relations with potential new buyers were concerned.
Question 3. What Canadian products were shown at this exhibition?
Answer: Some Ontario cheese and B.C. canned salmon was shown privately.
The answer the minister has given does not hold water at all. Canada cannot possibly expand her export trade on a basis of doing it perhaps some day, some month or some year. Surely this is good publicity, and it is good public relations to let your products, your brand names, be known, because we know the import restrictions and monetary situation are not going to remain as they are forever. Advantage should have been taken of this opportunity strictly for exhibition purposes, in my opinion, because that is good business.
This was not just a small exhibition according to all the reports I have received,

Supply-Trade and Commerce and I have more than just this one by Jack Scott. This exhibition is going all over the United Kingdom and has already been seen by millions of the buying public. These are the people who will eventually have to be reached by the importers of these goods from Canada, because they have to sell to the buying public. Surely it is good sense to try to have something from Canada in an exhibition of that nature.
I just do not follow the argument of the minister. As a matter of fact, whenever he does not like what a member of the opposition says he accuses that member of trying to run down Canada. We have just the same love for Canada that the minister has, and just as much interest, if not more, in the development of the country and seeing trade expanded, because we represent the working people of this country. We know they have to have jobs in order to eat, and in order to provide jobs you have to be able to sell your products.
I can tell you that we are never going to do anything that is going to hurt the working people of this country. Whenever we think there is something that can be done or should be done, we feel it is our responsibility to point it out right on the floor of the House of Commons or in a committee, and ask whether something more cannot be done that has been done in the past. I will not take second place to the minister or anybody else in my desire to build Canada, because I know that is the way to preserve jobs for the workingmen.

I just want to say one or two words here. I am not going to allow the earlier remarks of my hon. friend to pass. I implied no motives to him; I cast no aspersions on that article or the author. He is quite entitled to write any article that he sees fit to write. There is no contest here as to who is the greater patriot.
You are the one who started it.
It is just nonsense to talk that way. Let me tell my hon. friend that very often he takes some very small item and blows it up into a major issue; that is the point I was making.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There are two matters I should like to discuss very briefly, if I may, and which on their face may not appear to be germane to the minister's estimates, but on consideration and reflection I am sure it will be quite clear to the committee that they do fall within the ambit of the estimates now before us. I refer to two publications that are produced by the minister's department. One is from the dominion bureau of statistics, published under the authority of Hon. Gordon


Churchill, Minister of Trade and Commerce, entitled "Railway Operating Statistics", and is for March, 1959. The other is published by the same bureau, under the authority and jurisdiction of the minister, and is entitled "Employment and Payrolls, March, 1959".
My purpose in bringing up this matter at this time is that on a number of occasions we on this side of the house have been attempting to get information concerning layoffs on the Canadian National Railways. We have been unable to obtain this information either here or in the committee. However, there is very revealing information contained in these publications, and I should like to put just a short paragraph or two on Hansard and then ask the minister one or two pertinent questions.
The point I should like to make is this; that on page 6 of the March issue of "Railway Operating Statistics", which I now hold in my hand, it will be found that railway employment as of February, 1958 on Canadian National Railways stood at 87,554 employees, whereas in February, 1959 it was down to 82,427, making a decrease for that railway of 5,127. On the same page it will be found that railway employment on the Canadian Pacific Railway as of February, 1958 stood at 62,938 as compared to 59,084 employees in February, 1959, a decrease in that case of 3,854 employees.
Still quoting from the same publication, the total for 22 railways in Canada for February, 1958 appears to be 160,938 employees as compared with 151,086 in February, 1959, a decrease of 9,852. It will be seen from this that in the case of the Canadian Pacific the decrease is slightly over 6 per cent of the number employed in February, 1958, whereas in the case of the Canadian National the decrease represents a little less than 6 per cent. It seems to me it is significant that this information appears in a publication under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is significant, too, that this information appears to be so clear and definite.
I should like to proceed to a consideration of the other publication entitled "Employment and Payrolls". The figures here concern steam railways and I-

While this information may be important from the point of view of the Department of Transport, with respect I wonder what the purpose is, other than getting it on the record at this time, in reading these figures? It is true this publication is issued by the dominion bureau of statistics, and the minister is responsible for that bureau, but again with all due respect I wonder what the relevancy is?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The relevancy is this. I have already put certain figures concerning railway employment on the record, and I should like to put certain other figures concerning employment and payrolls on the record as well. Then I should like to ask the minister, as I indicated earlier, two pertinent questions on this material, because these are publications under his jurisdiction and the information contained therein has not been obtainable by us on this side of the house from the other department concerned.
Now, then, going to the publication "Employment and Payrolls" it appears that as of March, 1957 there were employed by the railways 170,014 men and women, as compared with March, 1958 when there were 158,041 employees and March, 1959 when there were 151,844 workers. For maintenance of equipment there were 24,604; 21,358; 19,927 for March 1957, 1958 and 1959 respectively. In so far as maintenance of ways and structures are concerned the figures are 32,830; 34,520; 32,934, for March, 1957, 1958 and 1959 respectively. In so far as transportation is concerned the figures are 102,744; 92,271; 89,317, for March 1957,	1958 and 1959
respectively.
Now, having put that information on the record, 1 would ask the minister these two questions; first, whether this compilation which is prepared by his department in these two series of statistics is done on a sampling basis; next, if not, whether it is done by an actual count. I think it makes a great deal of difference whether they are done in one way rather than the other, as I am sure the minister will realize this at once.
The other matter which occurs to me is this. Can the minister indicate to the house how it is that this information, which appears on the face of it to be quite simple, was not given by the Department of Transport in the first instance, or the other departments concerned? After all, there is no subject which is of more interest to all members of the House of Commons than these figures concerning employment on the various railways in Canada. There are few members in the House of Commons from one part of the country or another, who have not a divisional point of either one or other of the railways in their constituencies.
Now, sir, having dealt with that matter I would now like to deal with another matter which also concerns the Department of Trade and Commerce. That matter has to do with the commerce, the trade, and the business of the textile industry in Canada. As the minister knows the textile industry, in so far as its business and commerce is affected, has been very seriously hit and its operations very greatly curtailed within the last few 66968-9-388
Supply-Trade and Commerce years. I had the opportunity of putting certain figures on the record before. I shall not abuse the time of the house, but in order to deal with the matter rapidly would the minister allow me just to give some indication of what has happened to the trade in that field, particularly as it affects Canadian Cottons Limited. I am perhaps more conversant with that company than with any of the other companies, because for 19 years I represented a constituency in the house here where the cotton industry was very vital both to it and to eastern Ontario. In an article appearing in the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder of May 29, 1959 there appears this statement by the president of Canadian Cottons Limited, Mr. L. C. Bonnycastle. He stated:
Substantial reductions in operations, including the closing of some mills, are planned by Canadian Cottons Limited.
Total volume of sales was almost exactly the same last year as during the previous year.
That is 1958 as compared with 1957.
However, business has become increasingly competitive, prices have been low and the flow of imports from the U.S. and low wage countries have increased in volume.
Operations in Hamilton will be discontinued.
A little later on Mr. Bonnycastle states, dealing still with Hamilton:
The yarn mill will be closed and all activity in Hamilton will be discontinued by the end of the year.
The small yarn mill at Saint John, N.B., has been closed, and the Rosamond woollen mill at Almonte, Ontario, has been sold. There will be reductions in certain lines of products now made in Cornwall.
A little further on in the article it is stated:
"This means a substantial reduction in the work force in Cornwall within the next three months," a spokesman for Canadian Cottons Limited said this morning. He was commenting on the company's annual report, released today, which said the company was closing some of its mills and curtailing certain lines made in Cornwall.
But it was clear that a substantial number, perhaps close to half, of the 1,400 hourly rated and salaried employees of the Cornwall mills would be laid off by the end of the summer.
Canadian Cottons Limited has been operating in difficult circumstances for several years, due principally to competition in piece goods from U.S. mills, and more recently, made-up goods from Hong Kong and Japan.
Then follows an editorial, which I shall not read, which appeared in the same paper of June 11 of 1959, the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder. This paragraph only I would like to quote:
Exactly a year ago the Canadian cotton textile industry was undergoing an exhaustive review at the hands of the tariff board. After three months of hearings the board did not challenge the industry's contention that it was modern, efficient

Supply-Trade and Commerce and well-managed. Instead, the board suggested a complete reorganization of existing schedules covering imports.
Then it goes on to say that nothing was done to follow up recommendations of the tariff board.
During the last week I have obtained additional information as to the position in the Cornwall area, and I find that the mill is closing down completely as of tomorrow, July 17. Nine hundred and fifty men and women who make a variety of piece goods, flannelettes, saxonies, eiderdown ticking and the like, will be laid off tomorrow. I understand these lay-offs started some time ago, and they will be entirely completed with the mill closing down tomorrow.
To sum up, as recently as 1956 there were over 2000 employees actively employed in Canadian Cottons Limited in Cornwall, and after tomorrow, I am informed by a very authoritative source, there will be between 450 and 500 men employed. There are people in those mills who have spent their whole lives in the manufacture of textile goods, who are able to do very little else, some of whom have been there for years. In fact I was informed this week that in February 1959, 191 employees actively at work in the cotton mills of Cornwall had 25 years' service, and some of them averaged 33 i years' service.
I know these are not problems which have arisen overnight. I know full well, because I was close to the problem, that difficulties have been encountered over a number of years. But what I want to bring to the attention of the minister is this, that those who sit on that side of the house were quite clear, not only in 1957 but in 1958, that this would be put a stop to, and no one made more vigorous statements in that respect than the Prime Minister himself. I just want to put on record the statement he made in Cornwall on February 24, 1958, when he was quoted as follows:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker last night-
What is my hon. friend reading from, please?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am reading from a statement appearing in the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder dated February 24, 1958.
Prime Minister Diefenbaker last night promised that a Progressive Conservative government will bring in legislation to halt the "dumping" of textiles and other products in Canada.
Mr. Diefenbaker, speaking to an audience of more than 2,300 in the armouries of this textile centre, said Canada could not afford this and similar industries to be destroyed by dumping.
"We acted to protect the farmers of this nation against the dumping into Canada of agricultural products through the establishment of import controls", the Prime Minister asserted.

"Canada cannot exist without the textile industry. Following the representations to the tariff commission and on the basis of the recommendations of the tariff board, such action will have to be taken as is necessary to ensure that no industry will be subject to dumping," he added, bringing a burst of applause from the audience.
I wonder how that audience feels today when, a little more than a year after that statement was made, a whole mill has been closed putting 950 men and women out of work. Here was a definite promise to take action in this very vital field of trade and commerce, which actually was not taken. Then a little later on the following appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of February 25:
Mr. Diefenbaker followed the announcement about farm price supports with a promise his government will take whatever steps are necessary to protect the textile and other essential Canadian industries from competition from cut-rate foreign goods-an important issue in this textile manufacturing centre.
And a little further on:
Calling the textile industry "one of the great industries of our country", he said that in a foreword to one of the industry's publications last year, he has said the industry "had been subject too long to the innuendo of inefficiency" whenever it asked for better treatment.
And still further on in this article in the Montreal Daily Star appeared the following paragraph:
The tariff board was studying tariffs on the importation of textiles, and there was no reason why the government, after receiving its report, should not take action to assure no vital industry would be subject to dumping of foreign goods- the importation of goods for sale at prices below that in the country in which they were produced.
That is clear-cut evidence in 1958 which I have placed on the record, and there is evidence in 1957 as well, that no matter what had been done in previous years this government now in power would take the necessary action to prevent the curtailment of the textile industry. I say here without fear of contradiction that the position of the textile industry is worse today than it has ever been in its history, and the statement of Mr. Bonnycastle with respect to a whole mill closing down in Hamilton and another in Cornwall is evidence of that fact together with what I have put on the record.
I submit to the minister and to members of the government that now is the time to take action in this field. I do not want to be a demagogue and recall the promise made that no one should suffer because of unemployment. That promise was made by the Prime Minister, but I will not belabour it. I will merely say that there were specific promises made by the Prime Minister in the constituency of Stormont and in the city of

Cornwall in so far as the textile industry is concerned. Those promises have not been carried out.
It is true that legislation was brought in by the government concerning the dumping of certain of these products on the Canadian market. We made our position quite clear at that time. What has been the effect of that legislation? The effect of that legislation in so far as the Canadian cotton industry is concerned has been absolutely nil, because instead of the position being better it is far worse than it was before. I could go on. I have citations here which indicate the present state of employment in the textile industry, particularly in Canadian cotton production, but I do not wish to labour the matter unduly.

May I be permitted to ask a question? I come from a sizeable textile district, and I wonder if the hon. gentleman is aware, as he goes back over the years, that the unemployment situation in my textile riding on December 31, 1957 can be judged by the fact that there was 3,386 applications for benefits, whereas two weeks ago applications numbered 699.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, I was not aware of that, and I am very happy to learn that the position is such in the riding the hon. member represents. But I am aware of the position in the city of Cornwall, where I was last week, and I am aware of the statement which was made by the president of Canadian Cottons so far as the city of Hamilton is concerned, where 1,000 men and women will be without employment, and I think that is serious in the light of the promises that were made.
I would be only too happy if I could rise and make a statement similar to that just made by the hon. member. Unfortunately that is not the case, and here is the city of Cornwall, a community which has lived and thrived for many years because of the cotton mills. There were three cotton mills in that area. They are now reduced to one mill, employing between 350 and 500 men, and I think the time is now ripe for the government to live up to the promises and assurances they gave to that textile community in 1958 and in 1957.

I should like to say this in answer to the hon. member for Laurier. In the first instance, with regard to his question concerning publications by the dominion bureau of statistics and whether or not the figures were on a sampling basis or by actual count, may I say that the figures to which he referred in the publications he mentioned are actual counts and are not on a sampling 66968-9-388J
Supply-Trade and Commerce basis. There may be minor differences in coverage for all railways owing to the inclusion in the railway statistics of United States branch lines in Canada.
On the second subject with which the hon. member dealt, the textile industry in Canada, we are not by any means unaware of the difficulties facing that industry. I have received many representations from and held conversations with many people actively connected with that industry with regard to its problems. I do not wish to avoid any responsibility as a member of the government with regard to the problems which face the textile industry, but I think here, on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the hon. member for Laurier has raised a problem which goes somewhat beyond the departmental estimates. Some of the matters he dealt with are more properly under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue, and I would have thought that the hon. member for Laurier, if he were going to quote statements which he alleges were made by the Prime Minister, would do that in the presence of the Prime Minister instead of easing in these suggestions about promises which have been made and not fulfilled.
Let us keep the record straight. This constant needling about the failure of the government to keep promises is going to boomerang on hon. gentlemen opposite, because the record is there and the record is very clear. The promises that were made are being kept. They cannot all be completed within such a short space of time, but every single one is being met and will be honoured. Let the hon. gentleman not carry on these suggestions or insinuations that promises are made and there is no intention of keeping them.
Various steps have been taken. Even with regard to the textile industry, references have been made to the tariff board by the Minister of Finance. As the hon. member recognized, certain changes in the law were made which tend to ameliorate some of the conditions about which he spoke. The problem is being tackled and is being actively considered. As my friend the hon. member for Waterloo has just pointed out, the effect of the present policy is being shown to be advantageous in some areas of the country. It may be that there is a peculiar and difficult circumstance in the city of Cornwall. We sympathize with people who are placed in an awkward position or thrown out of work, but let not the impression be created that this is general across Canada.
The policy of the government is firm and sound. Those measures that could reasonably

Supply-Trade and Commerce have been taken in the time that has been at our disposal since March 31, 1958 have been taken, and we will pursue constructive policies leading toward full employment and the betterment of the condition of people not only in the textile industry but in all other industries.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister to give the committee an indication as to what has been done to meet the position as I outlined it in respect to the Canadian cotton industry?

Here again we have a question which should more properly have been raised with the Minister of Finance, who has referred some of these problems to the tariff board. This is not the primary responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words to brighten up the history outlined by the hon. member for Laurier. I also come from a textile city, and I am very glad to report that in this line of work business is much better than it was two years ago. The Goodyear Cotton company at St. Hya-cinthe, in recent weeks has hired or rehired about 125 hands, and since last year I would say at least 200 persons have been hired or rehired there. At the Yamaska Shirt company they are busier than they have been for a long time. At Penmans Limited the same situation exists and they are enjoying increased activity. At Consolidated Textiles Limited they are so busy they cannot give two weeks' vacation to their employees, and have to limit them to one week only.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some comments concerning what I thought were the rather unfair remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier. In the light of information that has come forward from other centres I am wondering if perhaps his statement, the validity of which I am not denying-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is undeniable. It is a fact.

Quite right. I am wondering, however, if the hon. member's statement perhaps concealed the true nature of the market. My hon. friend is quite aware of the changes that have taken place as a result of the introduction of new synthetic fabrics. For instance, in the men's shirting field there are entirely new products available, and perhaps garments made from them are not manufactured in the city of Cornwall. Every time someone buys a terrylene shirt it means that a certain amount of standard Canadian cotton material has not been used. My hon.
EMr. Churchill.]
friend has only to go into a men's haberdashery shop or a department store to see how many shirts of that type of material are available. I refer to garments manufactured of finer quality, non-wrinkle, no-iron fabrics. These are appearing on the market in vast quantities. I have referred to only a narrow segment of the industry.
I have no knowledge of the type of materials that are produced in Cornwall, but if they are manufactured of the more staple type of cottons or the standard type of shirtings I believe it is conceivable that the diminished markets may be the result of a change in the public taste as well. I think the hon. member should put all the facts on the record, and then determine whether all the decline in the market for these materials is necessarily the result of government policy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to reply briefly to what the hon. member has said. It may be that the suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton West is correct, and I am not denying the fact that the introduction of new materials has been detrimental to the demand for standard products. But the point is this. Has the hon. member forgotten 1957? If he has, I have not. In that year we were told in no uncertain terms that we were responsible for that situation. That was said by Conservative candidates who spoke in ridings where there are textile mills. Not only was it said by candidates but by cabinet ministers who came into the ridings, as well as by the Prime Minister himself, as I have indicated.
The point I am making now is this. Having said those things and having put the Liberal party in the impossible position of being expected to take the blame for a condition for which we were in no way to blame- the hon. member must admit that we made no promises in those years and the statement made by the Prime Minister was clear cut- I say it is now up to those who sit on the other side of this chamber to make the situation good in so far as the textile industry, at least in eastern Ontario, is concerned.
But you did not have the same situation at all.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for a moment about the subject mentioned a while ago. Now that a bid has been made by several hon. members in respect to the locating of the atomic energy plant for the development of hydro in their areas, I feel I should go on record as mentioning the action I have taken in respect to this matter.
Early last June I engaged in correspondence with Mr. Smith, assistant general manager in charge of engineering for the Ontario

hydroelectric power commission with respect to the possibility of locating the plant in my riding. I am happy to report that although the selection of a site has not been definitely made, testing is now under way in Bruce, and it is expected that other sites in our immediate area will be tested. I, of course, am still hopeful that it may be located in Grey North. I feel that we have one of the best locations in the province of Ontario. Already reports have appeared in the press concerning the possibility of it being located there.
I urge the minister to give consideration to the possibility of locating the plant in this area. I feel that my riding of Grey North has much to offer for this kind of project. We have solid rock and an ample supply of good cold water. Indeed, in Georgian bay I believe we have the coldest water available in the province. We have a sparsely settled area that is in close proximity to highly industrialized parts of Ontario and the area is served by good highways. I understand that these are some of the requirements for a site. I hope the minister will give my appeal the fullest possible consideration.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first time I have risen to speak on these estimates, and I shall detain the committee but briefly while I outline the plight of tomato growers and the tomato canning industry in British Columbia. I might say this industry commenced over 50 years ago because it is an ideal country for growing tomatoes, with warm summer months and ample water for irrigation. I remember when the first tomato plants were planted something over 50 years ago. The industry developed because its natural market-
They must be pretty old plants by now.

I may say, Mr. Chairman, that we do not think in those terms. We have a revival every year. I may say that the industry developed consistently over a long period of years, owing to the fact that it is a natural place for the growing of tomatoes and western Canada was the natural market. Until toward the end of the late 1940's they were processing some 26,000 or 30,000 tons of fresh tomatoes a year received from 500 to 600 primary producers, and some 1,500 to 2,000 persons were directly or indirectly employed in the growing of the tomatoes or in the canning industry. I think the peak value of the crop at one time was around $5 million; that is the total crop, those used for selling in the domestic market, largely in western Canada, and the remainder used in the canning industry.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
However, Mr. Chairman, the industry suffered from some severe disabilities, as I think the minister knows. I am bringing this to his attention because I have been asked to do it. First of all, the industry suffered from serious disabilities with respect to transportation. It may be interesting to know that the rate on canned goods from San Francisco and Los Angeles to Vancouver, about 1,000 miles, is almost identical with the rate from Kelowna to Vancouver or from Nelson to Vancouver. The rate from San Francisco and Los Angeles to Winnipeg, approximately 2,300 miles, is $1.80 compared with a rate from Kelowna or Kootenay points to Winnipeg, approximately 1,200 miles, of $2. These preferential rates on imported products were and still are prejudicial to the interests of the tomato industry in Canada, particularly in British Columbia. I mention it as one of the disabilities. I am not for a moment suggesting that this is a matter that can be solved quickly or overnight. It is one of those problems in which a number of factors are having an adverse effect on the industry.
Then there is the question of the higher production costs that we suffer because of the 25 per cent to 50 per cent higher costs for machinery and equipment; the 20 per cent to 30 per cent higher cost for cans; and the 50 per cent to 100 per cent higher costs for cartons, and a much shorter operating period for the industry in the interior of British Columbia. I may mention at this time that in the last two years five canning plants have been closed in the southern interior of British Columbia.
Then there is the question of tariffs. I do urge as a matter of consideration what appears to be certain inequalities which have developed as a result of the rigid operation of GATT which gives certain advantages to other countries because of their higher tariff rates and things of that sort. In that connection I am just going to quote briefly from this memo which was handed to me:
The American tariff of 21 per cent against canned tomatoes is approximately equivalent to the Canadian tariff of two cents per pound. The American tariff of 21 per cent on tomato paste is at least double the Canadian tariff on the same product and, when high concentrations of paste are taken into consideration, the American tariff rate of 21 per cent is over seven times as high as the Canadian rate. When the Canadian tariff rate on tomato paste was reduced in 1956 from two cents a pound to U cents a pound, tomato paste was being concentrated to a much lower percentage of solids, and the 11 cents per pound was equivalent to an ad valorem tariff of about 10 per cent. At the same time, United States had a 231 per cent tariff. Now, tomato paste is being produced to a consistency of 45 per cent-46 per cent solids, and the current California quotation is $21 per case of 45 pounds f.o.b. shipping points. The Canadian duty on a case of this products would be

Supply-Trade and Commerce 66 cents, or 3.1 per cent, against the present American tariff on the same product of 21 per cent ad valorem. If the United States tariff rate were applied to the American price, the duty would be $4.61.
In addition to that, Mr. Chairman, there is very unfair competition for our tomato producers and tomato canners in British Columbia developing from Italy and increasing over the years. The memo goes on to say:
We are aware of some imports of Italian tomatoes into western Canada, the total Canadian imports are heavy and increasing. With the low labour rates and other low production costs which processors in that country enjoy, along with low water-rates to the eastern seaboard and subsidized rail transportation costs from Canadian maritime ports, coupled with our extremely low tariff protection and unfavourable exchange situation, it is not surprising that many Canadian tomato processors are going out of business.
When they go out of business the producers of tomatoes will go out of business. Then, there is a very substantial loss of the export market. I am sure the minister is aware that prior to world war II the Canadian processors of tomatoes in British Columbia built up a considerable and substantial export market for tomatoes and tomato products. They have almost completely lost this market, together with substantially reduced tariff protection in Canada.
I am not going to deal at further length with this, Mr. Chairman. The minister must know the several disabilities that are being suffered by the growers and the industry in general. As a matter of fact, to show the committee the circumstances under which the industry operates at the present time, with all the increased freight costs and increased competition from the United States and other costs that I have mentioned, a 28-ounce can of choice tomatoes is selling today at 23 cents, which is less than the price was in 1948. It is impossible for the industry to carry on in these circumstances. I mention these facts and bring them briefly to the attention of the committee and the minister on behalf of the growers and canners of these products. I should like to know what the government intends to do in an endeavour to meet this situation and make it possible for these people to continue growing tomatoes and the canners to continue in business.
