Mr. Chairman, the minister was good enough when these estimates were brought before the committee last night to deal with many of the questions raised when 

the discussion took place on these estimates in the committee on June 25. He attempted to deal with the points I had raised in my remarks, but there are one or two aspects of these subjects on which I desire some clarification. Perhaps we now have come to the stage in the discussion where I can put specific questions to him and get specific answers.
I ought, first, to thank him for his remarks regarding trade with Japan. I had raised this subject, as had my leader, when the estimates were first before the committee on June 25. I was somewhat shocked last night when he was dealing with this subject to find, in looking at my own remarks on the earlier date, I was reported in Hansard at page 5812 as having said that barley exports to Japan for 1958 amounted to $62 million in value. This, of course, is the value of wheat exports to that country in that year, as I assume everyone who is really interested in this subject would know. I did not notice the mistake I had made until I was listening to the minister's remarks last night.
The question I want to ask him now is supplementary to the remarks on the subject of trade with Japan. There was a drop of some $35 million in our exports to Japan from 1957 to 1958, and in view of the importance of that market would the minister care to say or is he in a position to give us any indication as to what he expects our exports to that market will be this year? Will we have a chance to recover that loss?

The hon. member for
Ottawa West drew attention to the drop in exports to Japan last year and I think he will find the figures in the annual report on pages 26 and 27. I am reading from the report now:
The major decline in exports to Japan was in primary iron and steel products, particularly pig iron. This was the result both of expansion in domestic Japanese capacity and lower industrial output there. Sales of flaxseed which were unusually high in 1957 fell back to average annual levels. There was also a decline in Japanese demand for Canadian wood products, asbestos and aluminum. On the other hand the Japanese market for drugs and chemicals continued to expand.
In so far as the expectation for 1959 is concerned, the dominion bureau of statistics publishes "Canada, domestic exports" and the issue for May, 1959 on page 4 indicates the value in the period January to May of our exports in 1958 was $40,251,000. This value has gone up in 1959 in the same period to $44,924,000. Consequently I would say, in reply to the hon. gentleman, that we will regain our position with regard to exports to Japan.

I just want to express the hope, and I think the minister concurs with me in this, that the market can be built up in that area. In his remarks last night I think the minister indicated the importance he attached to that market. I perhaps do not need to elaborate on the subject here but I think the market for barley could be extended throughout that whole area.
There was another question I wanted to clarify arising out of an answer the minister had given to some of the earlier remarks I made about the West Indies. In the course of the minister's statement he made the remark that we have not increased our sale of fish and flour to the extent we would like. I presume he was referring to the sale of cured fish. I wanted to ask him, first, is that restriction in Jamaica on price still in force or has it been removed? Is there any prospect for increasing the export of that type of fish, not only to the West Indies but to the larger market that is to be found in the other Caribbean countries, Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico and so on? Would he care to develop that subject a little?

With regard to the price of fish and the situation in Jamaica, we are carrying on consultations with the authorities there. We hope to have a satisfactory answer in the near future. Prospects for the enlargement for the sale of our fish in the Caribbean and elsewhere are not unreasonable at the present time. We have, through our commercial counsellors stationed in those countries and through normal trade connections of our people engaged in the export of fish in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and so on, been able to maintain the trade. You will recall that a year ago we had some success with a very substantial order from Brazil. We are of the opinion that we can maintain our trade in fish with the West Indies and Caribbean region generally. The Department of Fisheries is taking active steps to make sure that the standard is maintained and that the method of processing the fish is improved. When the estimates of the Department of Fisheries are before the committee perhaps questions along that line will be raised.

Perhaps I can pursue the subject on the fisheries estimates. I wanted to raise another matter that concerns me and which I had mentioned earlier. It is from the policy aspect of the disposal of surplus farm products that I intend to attack the question. I obtained information by way of questions on the order paper and orders for returns tabled in the house on 66968-9-389
Supply-Trade and Commerce February 18 covering purchases by the government of agricultural products which were sold abroad by the Canadian government other than through the agency of the wheat board. One answer dealt at considerable length with skim milk powder and the export of that product to a great number of countries. I think there were some twelve or fifteen countries listed to which we had sold milk powder and the sale prices ran from about 20 per cent to about 75 per cent of the cost.
I asked another question about the export of eggs which were bought under the prices support program and sold to Venezuela. The price at which they were sold was again below the price at which the Canadian taxpayers bought them and there was a loss on that transaction. If I remember correctly, the price was something of the order of 65 per cent of the cost, although I could be out in that percentage.
Then I asked a question on the orders of the day on the subject of the export of surplus pork, and my question concerned the sale of surplus pork to Czechoslovakia. I received an answer from the Minister of Agriculture to which I shall make reference in a moment. Then I put a further question on the order paper and the answer was provided today and will appear in today's Hansard. The question concerned the sale of surplus pork, and it becomes apparent from the answer that we have so far been able to sell some of this surplus pork which the government purchased to three countries, namely Mexico, Italy and Czechoslovakia, and there appears to be a wide range of price from 16 cents to 30 cents per pound. However, it appears from the answer that it was again sold at a considerable loss below what we paid for it.
The point I am seeking to make on this matter has to do with the trade policy of the government. It will be seen from those three answers that we have sold surplus farm products at very substantial reductions below their cost to some 18 or 20 countries. In some cases we are selling them as little as 25 per cent of what the Canadian taxpayers pay for them. That, I suppose in any other country, certainly in Canada, would be termed as dumping.
The point I wish to make here is this. Does the minister consider that that is an appropriate permanent policy for the disposal of agricultural products from this country? What is its effect going to be on our trade generally? What damage does it do to the trade practices which we built up over the years? I think generally speaking our trade practices are regarded rather

Supply-Trade and Commerce highly. Does it take away from us any argument we might have against other countries for dumping products on the world markets and thereby hurting our sales?
Then I want this one further aspect of the matter clarified. In answer to the question I asked on June 21, as appears on page 4993 of Hansard, concerning the sale of surplus pork to Czechoslovakia, the Minister of Agriculture said, and I only want to quote part of his answer:
This is to some extent in the nature of what you might call a trial shipment and we hope that as a result-we are quite sure the pork will be found satisfactory-we shall be able to sell in constantly increasing quantities pork and other agricultural products in the European market.
What I would like to have specifically clarified is this. Am I to interpret that answer of the Minister of Agriculture as meaning that the Canadian government has now embarked upon a policy of seeking to increase exports of pork and other agricultural products to the European market by the direct subsidy method, as was done in the disposal of this surplus pork which had been acquired under our price support legislation? I think this point should be clarified because of its significance in the trade world.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member's final question as to whether the Canadian government has now embarked on a policy of increasing our trade by direct subsidy, the answer is no. This is not launching out into a new policy aimed at the expansion of trade through this particular method. It is, I would say, an ad hoc arrangement in a time of surplus, which is something that is not new. It has been tried in other years, the selling abroad of some surplus products from this country.
In answer to his general statement, I did to a certain extent deal with this last night, and I would say that the hon. member has laid his finger on the problem involved here. He asked, is there a danger of damaging the trade relations which have been built up in the past? Is there a danger that we may be accused of dumping surplus products abroad, and things of that nature? That is the nub of the matter indeed, but I would say as a general answer that we are very much aware of the effects on international trade of practices which deviate a bit from the normal and we are being very careful to do nothing which will interfere with the good relations that we have established with trading partners. We have been able to consult readily and effectively with countries which might be concerned with activities on the part of Canada with regard to surplus disposal.
As an example of that, I might say that in the gifts of wheat and flour that we have
[Mr Mcllraith.]
made to India and Ceylon we have been very, very careful to consult in advance Australia before taking any action whatsoever. The reason we have consulted with Australia is that those countries are the normal market countries for the sale of Australian wheat and flour, and the policy of the department is that no surplus disposal of wheat or flour shall take place in markets such as that without consulting with the countries primarily concerned, in this case Australia. Similar situations prevail elsewhere, and the activities to which my hon. friend has referred with regard to skim milk, the sale of eggs and the sale of pork are conducted very carefully so that our general trade is not damaged.
I might put on the record one or two further statements to make it quite clear. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, outlined to the House of Commons on April 23 the problems arising out of the accumulated surplus of dry skim milk and the steps that had been taken to reduce this surplus. Excess stocks have now been reduced to manageable proportions by sales of older stocks of skim milk powder for feed purposes and the stabilization board has withdrawn offers for export as feed although some quantities are still being made available for human consumption to international relief agencies and to governments for relief purposes. By offering this surplus product for export as feed the stabilization board was able to move large quantities of the older powder into export markets quickly in order to avoid deterioration of the product, and at the same time we were able to satisfy other exporting countries that these sales at concessional prices were not seriously interfering with their normal markets which are primarily for powder for human consumption.
With regard to pork, pork products are not among the items on which restrictions have been eased up to the present time- that is, with regard to the United Kingdom- although a number of countries have shown interest in obtaining supplies from Canada, in particular Czechoslovakia. A recent sale has been made at or very near to the world price, and it will represent the first time in many years that Canadian pork other than canned pork has appeared in the European market. Then the hope was expressed that this trial shipment might lead to further orders, which is the normal hope under circumstances such as these. If this food is found acceptable in Czechoslovakia, perhaps the market there may be developed.

I thank the minister for his statement, because I attach considerable importance to the clarification of this matter in view of the fact that since the first of the

year we have exported these surplus farm products to more than 20 countries. That, coupled with the statement of the Minister of Agriculture in answer to questions on the orders of the day, was capable of an interpretation which would be damaging to our trade, certainly if it was the policy of the government.
I have just two more questions with which I want to deal. One has to do with the statement made by the minister regarding the increase in our exports to the United States. I think the minister should have followed his own D.B.S. statistics more completely in the statement he made with regard to exports to the United States, and given the committee the whole story as to our exports. He told us that exports in the period between January and May of 1959 amounted to $1,186 million as compared with last year's total of $1,135 million. If the minister had gone on and given all the exports, the committee would have seen that exports to the United Kingdom were down a bit, that to the other commonwealth countries they were down some 25 per cent and that to all other countries, excluding the United States, the United Kingdom and commonwealth countries, they were down a bit, and that the total exports for those five months are down from last year. All I want to do in indicating that is to try to give a complete picture, because it shows the problems which do exist in this whole matter of export trade and the importance of this subject. We must keep pressing for markets as best we can all over the world and be very careful not to do anything which will interfere with those markets by any action or policy we may take.
I want to ask the minister for an explanation on another subject altogether. The estimates for this year fall, really, under six items apart from the board of grain commissioners, whereas last year the number of items was 15-I may be wrong about that number. In any event, there is a very sharp reduction in the number of items and there is a corresponding abbreviation in the details given in the latter part of the blue book. I want to ask the minister what was the reason for this change, because it seems to me that change is not an improvement but tends, rather, to make it more difficult to find the type of information which members of the House of Commons would wish to have when dealing with the estimates. In this one year it does, of course, make the comparison much more difficult and it does seem to me that the detail given in the present form is considerably less; practically all the departmental matters are shown under one item, that of departmental administration, and detail which 66968-9-389J
Supply-Trade and Commerce we had expected to find is no longer there. Could the minister tell us why the change has been made?

That is a fair question. There has been a change. This change was brought about at the suggestion of officers of the Department of Finance who are concerned with drawing up and publishing the estimates. A number of separate accounts have been eliminated and the bookkeeping has been simplified, but there is no intention to withhold any information whatever, and I find that the detail in the book of estimates does not differ very much from what was given in past years. The annual report covers the territory completely, and the combination of the two, studied by anyone who is interested in the subject matter, does, I think, give a full and complete picture of the department.

I hope the minister will practise some determination and stubbornness when he is dealing with the other department on this matter, because while the Department of Finance may wish to have them in a certain form for its own purposes I think, after all, it is the House of Commons which must be satisfied.

I do not want to put the blame on the Department of Finance. Our own officials were in agreement about this change; indeed, they might have been the ones who proposed it. I will take the full blame for the change, anyway.

In any event, I merely want to point out that changes should not be made merely for the sake of administrative convenience. It is the House of Commons which must exercise control over expenditure, which requires this information and it must always be borne in mind that this is the criterion which should be followed in setting these estimates out.

I am in full agreement. After all, this is information for the House of Commons, but I must, in fairness to the officials, say that I discussed this matter with them some time ago and I agreed to this modification.

Following along the same
lines, I have been wondering whether the minister would say where the details are to be found with regard to assistance to small business. A specific amount was shown last year.

It is not specifically set out. It is embodied in the general item 380.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I notice that in the annual report of last year the following appeared at page 72:
By the end of October an assistant director and three research officers had been appointed to determine a program based upon these terms of reference and to make recommendations concerning the staff requirements for such a program.
It goes on to say that the branch's initial functions have been concerned with a review of studies relating to the problems of small business in Canada and in other countries.
I should like to know what is being done, and what action the government intends taking this year. I hope the minister will not be too sensitive if I refer to election promises. There were definite election promises made, and one of these promises was reported in a Canadian Press dispatch which appeared in the Montreal Star of March 18, 1958. The Prime Minister, speaking in the minister's own province of Manitoba, said the government would set up a special branch to help small business to obtain a fair share of government contracts and-these are the important words for my purpose this afternoon-financial aid to expand.
All of those who have anything to do with business are aware of the increasing costs with which small businessmen are being faced at the present time. Some of this is due to government action and government policy. The increase in taxes, the increase in contributions to the unemployment insurance fund, the higher interest rates which make borrowing more difficult and of course more expensive, all contribute to the problems of the small business man. I say this only to lead into the question I wish to put to the minister. Does the government intend to make long term capital loans available to small business this year or in the foreseeable future? Could I have an answer to this question?

Mr. Chairman, I want to
deal with this same subject. I raised this subject on June 21 and last evening as reported at page 6096 of Hansard the minister was good enough to say that this point had been raised and he thought it might be more properly answered when we came to examine the item in the general estimates.
Like my friend the hon. member for Nipis-sing I could find no item other than the administrative item that would justify the minister for making the statement about this new branch about which there is real concern. I am all the more concerned about it because if a statement is to be made I think it should be made to this committee at this time while these estimates are available for debate. Following our first discussion of the minister's estimates on June 21, an article in the Financial Post commented on the fact that the


program of assistance to small business had not been examined by the cabinet. That was a couple of weeks ago when the newspaper felt justified in making a comment with respect to lack of progress following the setting up of the small business branch.
I hope we are not going to find that just as soon as these estimates are disposed of, as has happened too often recently, we will receive from the department a statement as to what their plans are and the House of Commons having prorogued we will be deprived of an opportunity of making any comment to the minister concerning what he has in mind and what has developed since the branch was set up.
I am sure the minister is aware that the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, Incorporated, has been making representations along this line. I wish to quote from a letter sent to me by the general manager of this association which reads in part as follows:
This association has made the suggestion that a retail business capital loans act be set up tor the purpose of enabling retailers to borrow money for rehabilitation and expansion. We have suggested that the mechanics of such an act be similar to those of the Homes Improvement Loans Act,
i.e. that the individual loans be made through the chartered banks, with a government guarantee.
This could be done by authorizing the bank to advance 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the cost of the proposed improvement or extension of buildings, equipment, parking facilities, etc. The loans would be repayable over a period of years.
As we pointed out previously such a plan would not introduce any new principle into Canadian finance. Similar assistance has already been extended to fishermen, farmers, manufacturers, homeowners and home repairs, food processors, etc.
That is one medium through which something might be done. One recognizes immediately that perhaps the vehicle of the international development bank might be used by expanding the terms of the act.
One of the industries that has been making representations along these lines is the tourist industry. We know that Canada's position with respect to income from tourists abroad has been deteriorating in relation to the spending of Canadian tourists abroad. We have a substantial deficit at this time. The tourist association at its annual conference indicated that one of the reasons for this situation is that the tourist operator is simply not able to find money in this era of tight money that would enable him to improve his business in a way to attract a large number of foreign visitors, particularly from the United States.
The minister well knows that in addition to the promises we heard at election time to which reference was made by the hon. member for Nipissing, following the government taking office the Minister of Justice

addressed the annual meeting of the Retail Merchants' Association in Vancouver and they got the impression, as did the newspapers, that this government intended to do something along these lines. That, Mr. Chairman, was more than a year ago.
In addition to that we know we have just gone through a winter of extreme unemployment. If some expeditious action were taken along the lines my hon. friends opposite were urging, I think it would have been of tremendous advantage last winter in the matter of the creation of employment if loans similar to home improvement loans had been made available to small business for the improvement of business premises and the improvement of other establishments such as I referred to in respect of the tourist industry.
This is not a matter of not having sufficient notice of this. Last June and July a conference sponsored by the Department of Labour was held on the question of winter employment. Of the five or six recommendations made by that conference only one was adopted by the federal government. The only recommendation made by that representative gathering of employees, employers and government officials adopted by the government was the recommendation of contributing to certain types of work carried on in the wintertime by municipalities.
Another recommendation not adopted was that encouragement should be given to small businessmen to improve their plants by accelerated depreciation, and some assistance in the matter of finance for construction in the winter months. Nothing was done in this respect.
On August 30, 1958 the Financial Post took notice of this matter and published an editorial entitled "What Help for Small Business" which reads in part as follows:
The Ottawa government has done some vague talking about special help for small business.
Then it went on to say:
The United States small business administration (established in 1953) has been made a permanent federal agency, authorized to grant individual loans up to $350,000 at interest rates which have been cut from 6 per cent to 51 per cent.
In the minds of most of us, that is not considered assistance to small business. I referred to this general question the other day without going into detail. I continue:
In addition, $250 million has been provided for loans by the SBA to investment corporations formed to provide long-term equity capital for small business.
I suggest to the minister that this has been worthy of attention long before now. Many people who had some expectations of
Supply-Trade and Commerce the fulfilment of promises in this area were rather disappointed to find that the small business section was set up in the Department of Trade and Commerce. It was expected that if anything more than some free and gratuitous advice was to be offered to business across the country, and if something tangible in the nature of financial assistance was likely to be provided, this section would probably have been assigned to the Minister of Finance. In any event, we have this new branch which has been in existence since last autumn. If the minister has some views in this respect he should convey them now to the committee so that we will not find next week after the house prorogues that, as the Financial Post hints, the country then and only then will get some of the minister's views.

The hon. member for
Kenora-Rainy River expresses himself in a singularly un-operative way in suggesting that I have nothing to say with regard to small business, and that if I am going to say anything I will say it next week after the house has prorogued and then at the same time expects me to get up and answer his questions. Before doing so, I would like to say this. Last night I noted that questions with regard to small business had been raised and my intention last evening was to go ahead with a statement concerning small business because I thought it was a proper question to come up in the committee. The committee will recall that because we could not continue after ten o'clock without unanimous consent and one hon. member refused that consent we therefore had to discontinue.
Incidentally, that member is not in the house now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I object to this statement.
It was the member for Skeena who refused unanimous consent. Had we gone on a little longer I intended to say something about small business.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I object to the reference made by the minister to something that happened here in a previous sitting.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Can the hon. member point to any unparliamentary remark about the hon. member?

I was simply explaining to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River why I did not give a report on the small business branch of the department. I had intended fully to do that last night. In an attempt to terminate my remarks within five minutes I inadvertently-and I hope the hon. member will appreciate this fact-said that I

Supply-Trade and Commerce would deal with it when we came to the item in the estimates overlooking the fact that I would have to deal with it under item 380.
I thank the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River for drawing my attention to this oversight but I hope he was not suggesting that I was attempting to evade making a comment on this particular matter.
The minister would want to mention not only the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River but also the hon. member for Nipissing, who also spoke on this matter.

I was just coming to the hon. member for Nipissing. I noted his remarks this afternoon. I was intending to ask him whether he would give me the reference from which he was quoting concerning the statement alleged to have been made by the Prime Minister. I did not get the reference; I was not sure.
I will be delighted to do that. I said I was not going to use the reference until I saw the Prime Minister in the house. It was a Canadian Press dispatch of March 18 and carried from coast to coast.
Reported in what paper?
The Montreal Star.

That is the information I wanted. I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Nipissing on making this reference in the presence of the Prime Minister; whereas some of his colleagues over there this afternoon took advantage of the Prime Minister's temporary absence from the chamber to make remarks with regard to alleged promises. However, in this particular instance the hon. member for Nipissing I think recognized that the promise to set up a branch to deal with small business was kept, as were other promises that were made during the course of election campaigns.
.You promised to make loans.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, I am the member who made statements concerning a matter dealing with the Department of Trade and Commerce in which I outlined some of the statements made by the Prime Minister at the city of Cornwall. I was accused by the Minister of Trade and Commerce earlier and again now that I did not make those statements in the presence of the Prime Minister. I am not accustomed to making statements in the house dealing with any member when that member is not here. Unfortunately, I am sure the Prime Minister was out on other important business and was not able to be in the house; but

surely I should not be charged with any irregularity because I made statements concerning the Prime Minister in his absence which are quoted in newspaper reports. It is a perfectly proper thing to do even if the member is not in his seat.
Mr. Chairman, I was not suggesting any irregularity. In passing I was simply commenting upon the fact-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You mentioned it twice.

-that the Prime Minister would like to have this information. He is interested in all that goes on in the House of Commons, and the remarks of my hon. friends, particularly the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier.
Let me get back to the question of small business. The branch was set up after the house prorogued last summer and extensive studies were carried out along the lines that I have indicated in the terms of reference that were given to the House of Commons on September 3, 1958. Those terms of reference were:
1.	To act as a clearing house in referring inquiries of small business to the appropriate departments of the Canadian government or provincial and municipal governments and to various other organizations and institutions;
2.	To compile and distribute bulletins and reports on topics of general interest to small business including information on government procurement;
3.	To assist small business on request to obtain statistical, technical and other information on management, production and marketing problems;
4.	To undertake studies concerning small business, particularly for guidance of the government in developing new policies in this field and as background material for dealing more effectively with the problems of small business;
5.	In the course of its work, to consult and cooperate with educational institutions, representative business association and other private organizations.
That was quite a program of work for the branch. At the present time the branch has seven employees, including an assistant director and three research officers. The size of the staff has been kept small purposely during the initial stage of the branch's development until it is able to assemble information and make a report. The most important duties of the officers of the branch have been to advise on a program based upon the branch's terms of reference and the staff requirements for such a program. An important part of the work of the branch has been a review of studies relating to the problems of small business in Canada and other countries and with the collection of quantitative and qualitative material on the position of small business in the Canadian economy.
I will not read all of the information I have here but I will summarize it in this

way, that is co-operation with the dominion bureau of statistics, and through liaison with provincial governments a great deal of information has been assembled. Liaison was also established with the United States small business administration. Officials of the department visited Washington in March of this year and a very great deal of work has been done in this connection and, I think, a satisfactory piece of work in the space of less than 12 months since the branch was established.
My hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River dealt with the need for financial assistance to small business and drew attention to the assistance given by a similar organization in the United States which, of course, is much larger in size than anything we have in mind at the present time. Then he pressed us for rather more rapid action and again talked about what the United States has done. But the United States program of lending instituted in 1953 was preceded by a number of years of investigation of the subject and by the previous extensive experience of lending to small business by other agencies of the United States government. It was not something that was done just overnight. The United States drew upon the experience of many years before going further with its assistance program to small business.
Surely it is only reasonable to give us some time to assess the problem, assemble the facts and establish liaison with various organizations and governments throughout the country before we go further with regard to what is an important sector of our economy. We would not have set up a small business branch under the Department of Trade and Commerce unless we were interested and concerned with the problems affecting small business.
I give at this time a progress report. The branch has been set up. It is being efficiently managed. I think it has done everything possible in the course of the nine months which have elapsed since it was established, and in due course the branch will reach conclusions and draw to the attention of the government various things that might be done for small business. We decided that small business needed a certain amount of assistance and this is the way in which we are going about it. To date I think it has been very satisfactory.
The problems of small business will be analysed and a comprehensive statement will be assembled with regard to small business throughout Canada. At that stage, through the Department of Trade and Commerce, representations will be made to the government as to future policy concerning small business. Small business constitutes the
Supply-Trade mid Commerce greater part of the business of Canada. Of that we are quite conscious and within our means and within reason we want to do what we can to assist.

I wonder whether the minister would answer my question. It covers only one small respect of aid to small business. It was in that spirit that I quoted the reference of the Prime Minister to "financial aid to expand" which literally means capital assistance. Does the government intend to make long term capital loans available to small business this year or in the foreseeable future?

Before a complete answer
can be given to my hon. friend, as I stated last year when this was under consideration, we have to have the facts. It is the assembling of the facts and information that is the duty and responsibility of the small business branch and the senior officials to whom the branch reports, who subsequently report to me. I pointed out that in the United States financial aid to small business was only undertaken after years of investigation and experience in other bodies, and the same thing is going to be true in Canada. We have not said either yes or no with regard to this particular problem and are not going to give an answer one way or another until we have the facts before us. That is why I have given the house an outline of the investigation to be undertaken by the small business branch and covering the five points to which I have referred. I have indicated that within the nine months that have elapsed since the branch was set up and the officials assigned to their task they have made effective liaison and assembled a mass of information from the business world. In due course this will be drawn together and future policy will be announced.

I do not wish to pursue the matter unduly nor do I want to be offensive in any way but when the minister says that the government does not want to act until it has the facts is he suggesting that these promises and statements were made without the facts? What is one to conclude from what the minister has said?

My hon. friend is one of the most genial members of the House of Commons. I realize that he has never said anything in the house that could be considered offensive and I do not take his remarks as such. However, I do not quite understand the hon. member's question.
I will be glad to restate it.

Will he restate it and expand it?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Perhaps I can restate it without expanding it. The minister has maintained throughout his comments on assistance to small business that the government does not want to move until it has all the facts and finds out precisely what the problem is. By saying that is the minister suggesting that the promises to assist small business to which I have referred and which were made from coast to coast-I do not want to delay the committee by quoting them-were made without knowing the problems that small businessmen have?

On the contrary, the problems that have been facing small business over the years were known to us at the time of the election campaign to which my hon. friend refers. They were known to other people in the country too but no action was taken by those who had the responsibility of government at that time. It was because no action had been taken that we suggested that when returned to power we would take immediate steps to investigate-
To make loans.
-to get the facts and after the facts had been assembled would then take action.
No, no.

I think that is a sensible and sound course. I am sure that my hon. friend, who is a very sensible man, will agree that you must have all the facts at your disposal before you can develop a plan. There was considerable knowledge throughout the country of the problems affecting small business and it was the lack of action on the part of the previous government that caused us to bring about this improvement. We have set up this small business branch within the department, are studying the problem in an intensive manner and will have a very good solution to offer in due course.
I have one final question and the answer can be yes or no. Does the government intend to make long term loans available to small business this year or in the foreseeable future?

I thought I had answered that in the course of my remarks by saying that when all the facts are at the disposal of the small business branch and they have reported to me the matter will then be considered by the government. That is the situation.

The minister does not seem to have thrown very much light on the situation. The facts are that on March 18, 1958 the Prime Minister is reported as having


stated that a special branch would be set up so that small business could obtain financial aid to expand.
May I ask what you are reading from?

I am reading from Hansard for July 17, 1958, page 2341 where there is reference to a Canadian Press dispatch in the Montreal Star of March 18, 1958, quoting the promise made by the Prime Minister that this branch would be set up so that small business could get financial aid.
May I ask, is the sentence in the Star in quotation marks?

If the Prime Minister says he did not say it, perhaps he will deny it now. It has been repeated many times since March in this house and it has not been denied before. The minister now says the branch has been set up so it can accumulate enough facts to enable the government to decide whether or not the Prime Minister's promise will be carried out.

I think the Leader of the Opposition will find that this promise will be fulfilled in 1962. Unfortunately, I was called out for a few moments and I understand that in my absence the minister made a comment about some of the events of last evening. I say with regret that I was not here so I could hear them and I am not in a position to make any reply unless the minister, of course, wants to repeat the references he made since he chose a time when I was out of the house to make them.
The hon. member is rather inferring that I was passing some remarks. I simply stated facts, that is all, and I think they are recorded in Hansard.
The minister says he stated facts. I shall look in Hansard to find out what they were and then we will be in a position to determine whether they were facts or only half facts.

Carried.
The Depuiy Chairman: Order.

About a year and a half ago an announcement was made by the minister with respect to the trade commission in Hong Kong going to the mainland of China for the purpose, as I recall it, of studying the needs of the Chinese people in so far as imports and exports were concerned. I am sure the minister realizes the special interest that exists in British Columbia in the lumber industry and other industries concerning the possibility of extending our export sales in China. I wonder whether the minister would be able to give any detailed information to

the committee concerning what the trade commissioner in Hong Kong discovered about the possibilities of exporting to the mainland of China and any other relevant data covering the question of trade with China.

The hon. member for
Skeena has drawn attention to a visit made to China by our trade commissioner in Hong Kong. Subsequently, he was back in Canada and gave a full report of his findings on that occasion which appeared in our publication, "Foreign Trade". This report contained a complete account of his investigation of the trade possibilities in China. I recall that he urged that visits should be made by Canadian businessmen to China if they wanted to enlarge their trade. He pointed out that China operates under a state trading arrangement. There are, I think, sixteen state trading corporations in China, and it is through those state trading corporations that foreign businessmen have to make their arrangements.
The prospects for enlarging Canada's trade with China are not too good. In 1958 we sold 8 cargoes of wheat to China which was a welcome addition to the sales of our wheat during the course of that year. Our total exports in 1958 were just under $8 million, and most of that was wheat. The figures for 1959, therefore, will drop back to what they were before those wheat cargoes were sold. Nevertheless, through the activities of our trade commissioners and through visits of Canadian businessmen and visits of representatives of China to Canada, increasing trade may result. We have had other reports from our trade commissioners indicating interest in China with regard to enlarging its trade with Canada. Several prominent businessmen have recently, within the last year or so, been to China and have written extensive reports in our newspapers concerning their experiences. That is the situation concerning Canada's trade with China.
I just have one question to ask the minister. Could he tell the committee what the government can do to assist the tomato growers of British Columbia and the tomato canning industry?

The hon. member for Kootenay West gave us a dissertation with regard to the tomato crops in British Columbia and indicated some of the troubles facing the growers there. I think we are aware, and we have taken note of their problem. The hon. member drew attention to the freight charges from the United States to Vancouver and from points in Canada, and also drew attention to the tariff regulations. I would point out to the hon. member that although I listened to him with a great deal of interest
Supply-Trade and Commerce and although I appreciate the difficulties facing the tomato growers of British Columbia, this is a matter which is not the prime responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I shall be glad to discuss this with my colleague the Minister of Finance and representatives from British Columbia to see what assistance might be given, but trade and commerce has not prime responsibility in this area.

I have been sitting here for a couple of hours shouting carried, and I have finally been carried away to the extent of wanting to ask the minister a couple of questions. I wondered, first, whether he had received a report tabled in this house by the committee on mines, forests and waters and whether he had any comments to make on one of the recommendations which was as follows:
Your committee feels that Canada cannot afford to ignore a potential so great for lumber and pulp sales as is offered in the Orient and, therefore, it recommends that these markets be approached on an open-minded basis.
I imagine they feel an open-minded basis would be that no concern would ever be given to the ideology of the particular regime there. I wonder if the minister has any comment to make on that particular recommendation?

We have no inhibitions with regard to trading anywhere in the world. We do not set up any barriers. I have already drawn attention to the activities of our trade commissioners in, I think it is, 59 countries of the world. This proposal with regard to the Orient is very good. Mr. Chairman, perhaps I can answer immediately the questions raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. He asked about the shipment of grain from the lakehead, indicating that the quantity shipped this year had been below that of last year. This is a matter of very considerable importance.
From the opening of navigation to July 13, the latest figure that I have available, the movement of grain by water from the lake-head amounted to 105,570,000 bushels. This compares with 161,318,000 bushels shipped from the lakehead during the same period a year ago.
The grain movement during the first 60 days of the 1959 shipping season on the great lakes was disappointing. The reasons for this small grain movement were discussed before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, and the representatives of the wheat board who were present summed up the situation as follows, and I quote their statement as it appears in the report of that committee:
There are reasons for the delayed movement of grain from the lakehead. The seaway was a new experience for all concerned and in the early part of the navigation season there were unavoidable delays in the movement of vessels. Beyond this, however, a new pattern of inland shipping was being worked out both for grain and other commodities. For example, lake vessels were making the long trip to St. Lawrence ports rather than the short trip to Georgian bay ports. In many cases, grain and ore were moved in combination. No one could anticipate to what extent ocean vessels would utilize the seaway to move grain directly from the lakehead. All these problems are sorting themselves out and there is every indication that the 1959 shipping season will see an adequate movement of grain from the lakehead.
In the meantime, the board has had, and will continue to have, sufficient wheat in eastern positions to meet all export commitments.
Another factor was the early and continuing heavy demand for ore shipments. During 

the first week of July, however, lakehead grain shipments exceeded those of the same week a year ago and I hope we shall have the same results for the remaining weeks of the crop year.
It is obvious that the delay in the grain movement out of the lakehead will affect the final quota position in Manitoba and in parts of Saskatchewan. There are still over 20 million bushels of space available in eastern Canada and 1 hope that the vessel movements out of the lakehead will be sufficiently large to fill the greater part of this space, at least by the end of the crop year.
The wheat board said at that meeting of the committee that I mentioned, and they have reaffirmed subsequent to that committee meeting, that they think the crop year will end with delivery quotas of seven and eight bushels per specified acre. That, of course, as hon. members realize, depends upon steady grain loading until the end of the crop year and that steady grain loading is still going on. With two weeks still to go I think we may reach that quota position.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River also wanted to be brought up to date with regard to the export position concerning the principal grains. I hold in my hand the Wheat Review for June, 1959, which has just come off the press and which gives the figures for August 1 of last year to June 18 of this year. The export of wheat as of that date for the 1958-59 crop year to June 18 was 221,703,933 bushels; for oats, 5,423,824 bushels; for barley, 47,855,011 bushels; and for rye, 1,099,477 bushels; flaxseed, 12,572,616 bushels.

I have one question in regard to the wheat situation at the lakehead. There were a number of difficulties that the minister may be aware of in the early part of the season with respect to the facilities at the elevators for handling foreign ships. I believe this does not come properly as a direct responsibility under this particular vote and this particular agency but I wondered whether the board has made any study of the matter, and feels that there needs to be a re-assessment by the elevators of their loading facilities, so that these foreign ships of larger draft and greater size and with different types of hatches could be accommodated better at the lakehead elevators than at present?

That has been a matter of study during the course of the present shipping season and alterations have been made at some of the loading points already to accommodate foreign ships. I think that with the experience of this year all the necessary changes for loading of foreign ships will be

made before the next shipping season commences. It has been a bit of a problem but the people concerned are fully aware of it and in some instances have already made the necessary alterations.

One point that has bothered me is that when this problem first arose at the lakehead there was an immediate demand that the government do something about it and a lot of the responsibility was laid upon the government. I felt at the time that perhaps this was being too kind to the government and that this really should not be a government responsibility at all. It seemed to me that the government's role would be one of advice and perhaps suggestion and leadership. Could the minister outline just what the government's responsibility would be and, so far as these changes are concerned, are we to expect that the government is going to pay anything toward the changes or contribute anything in the form of a subsidy or anything like that?

That question has not
arisen. The government's responsibility would be considerable at a government owned elevator but, as my hon. friend is aware, these elevators are mostly owned by other parties and any alterations would be the responsibility of the elevator company.

Mr. Chairman, I asked the minister this morning what the government had decided to do with respect to sales of uranium. I understand that while I was out a number of other hon. members were very interested in getting the reactor established in their ridings. It was said that it should be in Algoma East, Essex East, Nipis-sing and several of the Newfoundland ridings. I am not speaking on behalf of these people who want the reactor as I think there are factors that will decide where it is going to be established, but I am interested in ascertaining from the minister what he or the cabinet have decided to do with respect to the matter of building CANDU.
The minister may disagree or agree but it has been suggested by newspapers that if we are going to continue the sale of natural uranium we are going to have to give some leadership in the construction of the reactor that will work with this type of fuel. There are several interesting things in the annual
Supply-Trade and Commerce report of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and I should like to read one or two paragraphs.
The preliminary design study, which was completed in 1957, estimated that CANDU could be built for approximately $60 million. The development costs were not included in this total, as it was not thought reasonable to load the cost of the first large station with all the costs incurred in development.
Stopping there, I think this raises an interesting point. I used the example this morning of the Arrow program having some similarity to the handling of our nuclear program, and it will be noted that there is a difference here. Maybe we have learned something and are not now including the development costs in the cost of the first CANDU unit. We are not told in the report what the development costs for CANDU were. The report continues:
The study also concluded that If the station were incorporated in a public utility system, and operated with an annual load factor of 80 per cent, the cost of power produced would be under six mills per kilowatt hour. In other words, the target in Canada for a station of this size might well be reached.
As a result of the considerable effort which has gone into the design and the associated development of CANDU, and the success to date of the NPD-2 program, there is now great confidence that the preliminary estimates on CANDU are realistic. Work will continue on the present design and development phase until this is completed. The construction of CANDU will then be considered. The station would take about four and a half years to build.
I suggested this morning that if we got at the program of building CANDU and established the first natural uranium nuclear plant of commercial value we would be able to produce power by 1964 from this type of plant. The minister disagreed with my statement. I said that if he got cracking on it we might do it in less time and that it might be done by 1963. I do not think an answer has been given whether or not we have gone ahead. The Financial Post has speculated that if we go ahead with this type of program we will be in the international uranium market but if we do not go ahead with it then the United Kingdom and other countries are going to make use of enriched uranium and our natural uranium will not be useable in the type of reactor designed to use that kind of fuel. I think the cabinet or whoever makes the decision for Atomic Energy of Canada Limited should indicate if we are going ahead with the program, if we have not already done so, and I think the people of Canada should know the decision.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo stated today that it would be of great advantage for Canada to co-operate with England in an

Supply-Trade and Commerce atomic development program. While I did not think of this idea myself, I believe it merits a great deal of consideration because it seems to me that we in Canada are faced with the expenditure of large sums of money for development when we are having a great deal of difficulty financing the development of our natural resources without going into industrial development as well. England, a country that is faced with a lack of power and energy in all forms, is in vital need of this type of plant. I can see the advantages, both political and economic, in Canada and the United Kingdom joining together to produce a form of reactor that will be satisfactory to both countries. I think the minister should tell the Canadian people now if he has any new thoughts on the matter and if and when he is going to do something about it. I should like to suggest to the minister that if I were he I would try to reshuffle some of these departments he has under his jurisdiction.

Under this new supplementary administration item I should like to ask the minister about the likely timing of the supplementary report on private and public investment that is usually issued by his department. Will that be available fairly soon?

That report was issued today. I am glad the hon. member had drawn attention to it. He will be very pleased with it, as I am, because it indicates that the revised figures in 1959 will be more than $200 million above the estimate which was presented early this spring and will exceed the total capital expenditure of the year 1958. The revised figure for 1959 is $8,555 million whereas for 1958 the capital expenditure was $8,417 million.
That represents a significant increase and plans for social capital spending have been little changed from those outlined at the beginning of the year and still involve outlays about 4 per cent above those of last year.


On the whole, the results of the mid-year survey of investment intentions reflect increasing business confidence. More new projects are being initiated than was the case in 1958. Where business establishments have revised their investment plans these revisions have been preponderantly in an upward direction. Respondents in the mid-year survey were asked to outline the reasons for any changes in investment plans. The most frequent reason given for expanding a capital program was that the longer run sales outlook had improved.
In summary, the accomplishment of present investment plans will mean that construction activity will reach record heights in 1959 and that spending for machinery and equipment will reverse the downward trend evident last year. While the year-over-year increase planned in capital spending is fairly modest the realization of the program outlined will involve a substantial increase over the rate of activity in the first quarter. It may be expected that capital expenditures will exert a strong expansive influence on the economy in the latter part of the year.

May I just say that I rather expected this information would be available about now. I had inquired and found that just about this time, and some times earlier, the mid-term estimate was available. I believe this is an illustration of howT this government is prepared to avoid giving to parliament the proper information before we are discussing estimates. If this question had not been asked I doubt that we would have got this information today. We would have obtained it after the estimates of the minister had been passed. He would have had this data released and the people in his department would have put out a good mimeographed publication assigned to three hundred or four hundred people and sent to the press.
The minister knows that he went a little far in March when he tabled the original public investment report and he was challenged on that report on both March 10 and 11. He blazoned to the press the thought that there had been an increase in the new year of $100 million in the aggregate of public investment. He ignored the fact that as a result of population growth and G.N.P. growth, everything else would be up beyond that percentage figure. On March 10 I asked a question of the minister. The record is there, and I am not going to belabour the committee with it. On March 11 the hon. member for Ottawa West asked a subsequent question, a factual question, and you will find that the minister in his reply evaded the essence of the question asked.

The point is that $200 million, with reference to that report which involves $8.4 billion, is just about a one-fortieth increase and everybody knows that with population growth the G.N.P. should rise, the Minister of Finance says, 7 per cent this year. This particular increase, which is a very important integral factor in the G.N.P., is up only one-fortieth. 1 think we should have had this interim report tabled in this house at the opening of the sitting this morning. It was available, and we were going to question the minister about it because I knew he would have a typewritten report even if he had not a printed copy. We would have obtained this information on the floor of the house only if questions were asked.
The point is it was available for publication, but only as a result of questioning do we get this information. These growth rates are so much under what is happening in the United States at the present time that they naturally cause a great deal of alarm to a great many Canadians. I hope the minister will indicate the segments in the economy in which this growth has taken place. I recall when he tabled his report on private and public investment in Canada for 1959 it actually showed the prospect of a decrease of $100 million. It was indicated that in the social field there was going to be an increase having regard to provincial and municipal investments, but in so far as federal responsibility was concerned there would be an expected decrease, particularly in the area of housing. I think the minister might give us a little more information about this because, as I pointed out in my question on March 10, there was a decline of $100 million notwithstanding a rise in population and a general expectation of the average growth from year to year. We can only regard this as a defeat, so I hope the minister will indicate from what segment of the economy he expects the $100 million which he forecast as a reduction will be overtaken. We now have a $200 million increase beyond his original forecast, and where does it occur?

speechtext: I must point out that I stopped the hon. member for Timis-kaming who was going on to another matter, and in fairness to him, of course, I had to draw the matter again to the attention of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I think you were quite right, and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is just hair-splitting as he was doing earlier when talking about this report, and trying to create the impression that there was some concealment. It is that I object to, because on June 25, as reported at page 5170 of Hansard, when the estimates of this department were introduced, I said this:
The customary mid-year review of spending plans is now under way. Although the final figures will not be available for another two weeks or so the results to date indicate upward revisions in anticipated outlays sufficient to raise total projected spending for the year up to and probably a little above the actual outlays in 1958.
My hon. friends had that information placed at their disposal on June 25, and now

Supply-Trade and Commerce they get up and say that I attempted to conceal some information from them. It was all there, and furthermore it is a good report which was released by the dominion bureau of statistics today. My hon. friends just do not like to receive good news. This disappoints them. When? The next session?

We had to be asked the question. I draw to the attention of my hon. friends that things are improving in Canada, and for that improvement business and government can take some of the responsibility and the credit. My hon. friends do not like good news, and that is why they raise this objection now.

Mr. Chairman, one point arising out of the minister's remarks which I think he owes it to the house to clarify is why he did not table the document today if it was available as he indicated it was, and available to him throughout the day. Why was it not made available to members of parliament dealing with the estimates of his department?

The minister said that on June 25 he told the house that this report was not yet completed, but the information when it was completed would likely indicate a very favourable situation, and that in a couple of weeks or so it would be completed. On the basis of that statement two weeks ago that the report might show something we are expected to accept now from the minister a final report at the end of his estimates, a report which has an important bearing on those estimates, and expected not to complain but to assume that two weeks ago he was speaking correctly when he said that the report might show that. The minister also said a moment ago that he would have come to this report eventually. When would he have come to the report? We are on the supplementary estimates now. On what item of the estimates would we discuss this? It is an important report which has not been shown to the House of Commons. I do not know whether it was given to the press or not.

Mr. Chairman, it was by sheer accident that the Department of Trade and Commerce estimates were not completed in June. I was prepared to go ahead with them but there was a change of program. By now they would have been completed, before this report was even printed and

published. Then my hon. friends would have cried blue ruin again. The economy is expanding and they do not like to hear about that.

Let me clear up one point. The minister obviously has had this printed report today. Why did he withhold it from the house? I ask him the question, why was it not tabled and distributed in the proper way?
Mr. Chairman, I am not withholding anything.
Why do you not table the document, then?
For all I know it has been tabled.
It is your duty to know.
It is tabled under the minister's name.
If my hon. friends want copies I think we can have copies made available to them.
Not as a concession at the end of the estimates, but as a matter of right.
Certainly as a matter of right. You are entitled to the document.

Even for the press.
