Item agreed to.
ATOMIC ENERGY Atomic energy control board-
37. Administration expenses of the Atomic Energy Control Board, $62,800.
Mr. Chairman, we have been going quite fast in the last few minutes, but I think this item deals with the atomic energy control board.

Mr. Chairman, shall I make a statement first? I did not realize we had reached vote No. 37 with such dispatch, but I have a statement to make about the atomic energy control board, which is item No. 37 and is distinct, of course, from Atomic Energy of Canada Limited itself. It is a very short statement on this control board.
With the uranium producing industry in full operation, and with most of the information relating to peaceful uses of atomic energy declassified, the board's duties in connection with prospecting and mining and with security matters have been lightened considerably. Its responsibilities in health and safety matters, however, have increased, partly because of the increasing use of radioactive isotopes in industry and medicine, but mostly because of nuclear reactor projects outside of Chalk River.
Three of these have been dealt with; the nuclear power demonstration plants, a 20,000 kilowatt nuclear electric power plant at Des Joachims on the Ottawa river, a one megawatt swimming pool research reactor at McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario, and a sub-critical reactor-or more properly, assembly-at the University of Toronto. The
Supply-Trade and Commerce board has set up the reactor safety advisory committee to advise it on the health and safety aspects of reactors, and on the advice of this committee, given after intensive study of each project, has issued a construction permit for the first, and construction and operating permits for the other two.
In connection with CANDU, the 200,000 kilowatt power reactor referred to in my statement to the house on June 18 last, the selection of the site will be made by Ontario hydro subject to approval by the various other bodies concerned and by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and the committee will review the health and safety aspects of any proposed site before a construction permit is issued.
Another matter that is growing in importance is the export of uranium under the arrangements announced last year for export of sample quantities, under bilateral agreements with friendly nations, or through the international atomic energy agency. Under the act and regulations the board has to give final approval for these exports and must in this connection keep closely in touch with the other agencies concerned, particularly external affairs, trade and commerce and Eldorado.
That the board with its very small staff has been able to deal effectively with the matters in its charge is, of course, very largely due to the co-operation it has received from other government authorities, federal and provincial, and from the public.

I have already spoken about this particular matter, to which I think great importance should be attached, and there is not very much I would add to what I said this morning, but I should like to pay my tribute to the scientists and the engineers who are responsible for this nuclear reactor CANDU and to express the hope which has been expressed by the hon. member for Timiskaming that the nuclear power plant will be put into operation as quickly as possible, indeed if that is not done we shall be left behind, since the United States and the United Kingdom are making great progress in this field and in the export of their reactors and their knowledge to other countries. I think we must admit that they have some advantages over us, particularly the United States, because of the terms they can offer.
I was reading only the other day that nuclear power development in the United Kingdom had been carried so far that another station was about to be built, I think, in Dungeness. I also understand that our particular reactor is as efficient, as economical and as advanced, if not more so, than any

Supply-Trade and Commerce other in the United States or the United Kingdom. We have, if I may put it this way, a good product and it is very important to get that product into the markets of the world, and in doing so to assist those who are concerned with uranium in general.
The minister has mentioned that the site for the nuclear power plant has not yet been decided. He has received a good deal of advice this evening as to where it should be erected, but I take it from what he has said that the federal government is only one of the agencies which will determine the site of this establishment; Ontario hydro and Atomic Energy Limited will also have something to say about it. I would only repeat, as the hon. member for Nipissing is not here tonight, that there are very definite advantages attached to a site near Elliot Lake not only technically and from the point of view of the availability of material but because this is a community which is living now in conditions of insecurity arising from the possibility that contracts with the United States will end in 1962. During this intervening period of uncertainty it would really mean a great deal to that community, which is the centre of the uranium district in this country, to have the plant in that area. But that is, of course, something which the minister and the other levels of government together with the Ontario hydroelectric commission will have to decide.
We are now on the verge of great developments in this field, not only in the military but in the non-military uses of nuclear energy. We in Canada have certain advantages, not only as to the material used but because of the skill and knowledge of our scientists and engineers who have developed a plant which is second to none in the world. I am sure that the government as well as all Canadians will wish everything possible to be done to ensure that our country remains in the forefront of this development which is fraught with such great possibilities not only for ourselves but for the rest of the world.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to follow up what the Leader of the Opposition has said by asking the minister what the position is with regard to the development of power from atomic energy. He made a short statement on this subject a moment ago, but I should like to know exactly how far we have advanced in development of power in this field. What is the cost of the reactor? How much will be contributed by the federal government, how much by Ontario and how much by the hydroelectric power commission. Further, I should like to know-and this may be a question that cannot be answered


at this time-how the cost of the development of one horsepower from atomic energy compares with that of developing an equal amount of energy from water power.

I made a short statement on the atomic energy control board which is the item we are now considering. Item 39 deals with Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. I do not think it is material whether we restrict our discussions to the control board. I think that last year we ranged the field and then passed the four items one after the other, so I will now proceed to make a statement concerning item 39, namely, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Then perhaps I will answer some of the questions which have already been asked, and subsequently I will endeavour to answer some other questions.
I think there was a misunderstanding earlier as to the program. The hon. member for Skeena was reading from the annual report of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited which came out in May, and the program for proceeding immediately with CANDU was announced in the House of Commons on June 19, and I think this led to a measure of misunderstanding as to what was being done. But with regard to the program of atomic energy development generally in Canada I would like to say a few things.
The present Canadian power reactors being built and designed are a direct evolution of the work at Chalk River, starting with the original zero energy reactor in 1945. This was a heavy water moderated experimental facility and it is still used for basic reactor research. It was followed in 1947 by the very successful NRX reactor which is heavy water moderated and cooled with ordinary water. This reactor has proven to be one of the best research and engineering test reactors in the world. The NRU reactor followed in 1957, with five times the power of NRX, accomplished primarily by arranging for cooling with heavy water. It has been working very well for the last six months, following a period of start-up problems. It is the first reactor in the world to change fuel under power, now a routine operation.
The prototype power reactor NPD-2 which is under construction and due for operation in 1961 is heavy water moderated and cooled, as will be the first full-scale plant, the 200 megawatt CANDU recently approved for construction. All of these reactors are fuelled with natural uranium.
Concentrating on one basic system has allowed our scientists and engineers to become thoroughly familiar with all the detailed advantages and disadvantages of the system.

They are recognized throughout the world as being the best qualified group in this particular field. It is to our advantage that we have stayed with one line and it is not because we have refused to look at other reactor systems. There is nothing mysterious, to the scientist, about the other systems such as the graphite moderated reactors so well developed by the United Kingdom, or the light water enriched reactors developed mainly in the United States. Although our knowledge of these systems is not as intimate as it is with the heavy water systems, through our associations with scientists and engineers in the United Kingdom and in the United States we have a good understanding of what is involved and can make reasonably valid comparisons between the Canadian approach and that of other scientific groups. The technical staff at Chalk River are continually reviewing new and promising reactor concepts and to date have seen no reason why we should change our present approach.
Having established a position as one of the five leading nations in atomic energy development and having become particularly well qualified in the heavy water field has had its effect on the interest of other nations in the Canadian program and in the Canadian establishments as a training base. The advanced countries such as the United Kingdom and the United States are interested in joint programs of basic research or fuel development or even reactor designs, whereas the lesser developed countries are more in need of general training for their scientific staff.
The program of co-operation with the United Kingdom and the United States is extremely close and fruitful. Both countries have about fifteen personnel stationed at Chalk River. We have a long history of excellent co-operation with the United Kingdom, particularly in the research field where there has been a continual exchange of staff between Harwell and Chalk River for a number of years. More recently much closer collaboration has been agreed upon in the applied programs of reactor development in both countries. Technical staff from the United Kingdom atomic energy authority industrial group are working closely with their opposite numbers at Chalk River. A joint project associated with the design and development of steam cooling a heavy water moderated reactor has been inaugurated. The United Kingdom reactor designers recognize the merits of heavy water as a moderator and are active in design studies using this material. Chalk River have two experienced professional staff assisting on this work at the United Kingdom industrial group design office. The UKAEA are quite cognizant of
Supply-Trade and Commerce Canada's advanced position in heavy water reactor development and are relying to a considerable extent on some of our experience, particularly that related to fuel development and the general problems associated with handling heavy water.
The co-operation with the United States has been very close and very broad from the start of the program in Canada. The whole of the uranium oxide fuel development work which is an essential part of the power reactor program has been closely allied with projects of the USAEC. The Chalk River reactors NRX and NRU are ideal test beds for fuel development and the NRX reactor, particularly, has been used to a maximum degree. The United States atomic energy commission has co-operated to the extent of supplying major pieces of equipment and a steady flow of special fuel specimens. The results of all the work are shared, regardless of where the project originates, which has undoubtedly assisted in reaching the present advanced stage of the oxide fuel development.
The USAEC has recently shown special interest in the power reactor development program in Canada. They are placing engineers on the design teams on both the organic cooled heavy water moderated study, as well as the CANDU project. This is in addition to the staff normally located at Chalk River and is indicative of their interest in the heavy water system for nuclear power. Although the USAEC has pioneered the work on organic coolants and will have much to offer the Canadian project, they have not, to date, proposed a reactor project coupling organic coolant with heavy water moderation. The Canadian project will be a very important link in the over-all development of the organic reactor systems. The USAEC will be developing two other systems utilizing organics and the heavy water moderated system fills an obvious and very promising gap. A full exchange of information on each of these projects has been arranged.
Co-operation with India needs special mention. As is well known, Canada is providing India with a large research reactor known as the CIR-Canada-India reactor

under the Colombo plan. This reactor, similar to the NRX reactor at Chalk River, is scheduled to go into operation next spring or early summer. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is providing extensive technical assistance in connection with this project, including the training of the Indian operating and maintenance staffs and in the preparation of the necessary handbooks and manuals. Thirteen engineers are now at Chalk River receiving training of this kind.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Owing to the shortage of working accommodation at Chalk River, AECL has had to limit the number of staff from other countries attached to Chalk River, but during the past year it has been possible to accept one or two scientists and engineers from about twelve of these other countries to stay at Chalk River for extended periods. To meet the need for training larger numbers of qualified staff from Canada and abroad, a reactor school is being established at Chalk River. The first course will be given early in 1960. An announcement about the reactor school will be made shortly by AECL and a prospectus will be issued to all organizations likely to be interested.
While atomic power will no doubt become the most important peaceful application of atomic energy, the uses of radioisotopes in medicine, agriculture, industry and research are also very important and far-reaching advances are steadily being made. The commercial products division of AECL processes and sells the radioisotopes produced in the Chalk River reactors and designs and develops equipments using these radioisotopes.
The principal source of revenue of the division continues to be the sale of Cobalt-60 and Cobalt-60 beam therapy machines. There are now six models available and 147 have been sold to 27 countries. A new Caesium-137 unit is also now being made on a production line basis. This machine is of special benefit in the therapy treatment of growths close to the skin. Another new item of equipment being marketed by the commercial products division is the Gammacell 220. This is a completely shielded semi-mobile unit containing a very high activity Cobalt-60 source for use as a development tool or an industrial radiation source.
Revenues of the division were down slightly during 1958 owing to a decline of foreign orders, but in recent months new orders have shown a definite improvement. As a result, it appears that the volume and value of sales will continue at the rate of about $2,500,000 per annum.
As I announced in the House of Commons on June 17, the success to date of the work on the small power reactor coupled with the results of further experiments by the scientists at Chalk River and the design work of the engineers in the nuclear power plant division located in Toronto, has been such that a decision has been taken to proceed with the final design and construction of a full-scale nuclear power plant. This rounds out Canada's nuclear power program which may be summarized as follows:
The 20,000 kilowatt NPD-2 project is expected to be in operation in 1961 and


will give Canada an early demonstration unit and will be particularly useful in the development of fuel cycles and the general development of reactors of this type.
The 200,000 kilowatt CANDU is scheduled for completion in 1964 and will be our first full scale power reactor. This design will rely heavily on the design of NPD-2 and, exclusive of design and development costs, it could prove to be an economically competitive unit if it is operated in the Ontario hydro system as a base load station and is competing with imported coal.
The OCDRE, organic cooled deuterium reactor experiment, design study fills several roles in the program. It may be considered as a "back-up" to the NPD and CANDU type of design where an organic material replaces the heavy water as the coolant. One of the specifications covering the design is that the steam produced from the reactor is of a quality which could be used at a northern site with Frobisher Bay as the preference. It is quite possible that this system would produce the most economical plant of all for small stations fueled with natural uranium. It is quite reasonable to expect this design to produce the best natural uranium fueled plants in sizes up to about 150,000 kilowatts, electric.
A project to study the enriched systems for application in very small sizes at remote Canadian sites is under way. This project consists of a study contract relating Canadian load and site conditions to the reactor designs and prototype plants which have been thoroughly investigated in the United States. The Canadian contractor is obtaining full cooperation from the relevant United States sources. This study should give us the answer as to which system would be most economic for application to remote sites. The project is jointly sponsored by AECL and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Although these power reactor projects are a major portion of Canada's program we should not lose sight of the importance oi the work at Chalk River associated with the general research and development program. This is really the hard core of all atomic energy development in Canada and without this large fund of knowledge and experience the power reactor designers would soon find themselves faced with problems beyond their experience and competence. This establishment is costing the government of Canada from $25 million to $30 million a year. Part of this could be assigned to the specific task of developing nuclear power but there is also a large part which is needed to keep Canada

in the forefront of nuclear development. I think that all will agree that the money is being well spent and certainly those who have had an opportunity of visiting Chalk River will approve of this expenditure.
The staff is generally quite young: they are vigorous and competent and measure up well with any similar group anywhere in the world. Canada gained the enviable position of a leading nuclear nation during and immediately following the war. It is the scientific and technical personnel and the support they are getting which is keeping us in this position.
The estimates for 1959-60 follow right along with the program outlined in my policy statement of February 1, 1958, and my statement of September 3, 1958 on last year's estimates. The total of $31,379,500 consists of $7 million for the NPD-2 project and the design and development work on CANDU and approximately $24.4 million for Chalk River. The effect on the estimates of the approval of the CANDU project will not be seen to any extent this year other than through commitments.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a couple of points. With the blessings of the coming of industry, and particularly the mining industry, we have always had dangers in certain mines such as occupational hazards or illnesses pertaining to that particular mining industry. For example, there is the illness caused by gas and the danger of explosions, and so forth, in the coal mining industry. We have always had the scourge of silicosis in the hard rock mining industry. A great number of people from my riding have left there to work in the uranium mines in various places such as Bancroft, Blind River and elsewhere. Many of them have left their families there and they come home from time to time; they move back and forth. There is always a lot of talk. I do not know how much of it is true, and how much of it is embellished, about the dangers involved in radiation, and so forth, in the uranium mining industry. Can the minister inform the committee as to what has been the experience to date, just what hazards peculiar to this mining industry have developed and what steps the government has taken to combat those hazards?

I am informed that there is no special hazard attached to the mining of uranium that differs from other mining activities. There is the question of control of dust, and the mining authorities institute the proper control systems and the provincial governments exercise supervision over those precautionary measures.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Does that apply as well to the processing? In other words, from experience there has been no instances of radiation poisoning or anything of that nature in the mining process or in the processing of the ore afterwards?
There is no radiation hazard in the processing operations.

Can the minister tell me whether he has any information at hand with respect to this matter? He mentioned that 167 cobalt bombs were sold to 37 countries. Can he tell me how many of those cobalt bombs were purchased out of funds provided by health and welfare for use in Canada?
That is important information which should be made available and will be made available to the hon. member but not immediately. We will send word to him tomorrow.
The former secretary of state for external affairs, who should know about the number of countries, informs me that I was not correct when I said 168 countries. I should have said 37.

I just have one question and it is related to the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Japan for co-operation in the peaceful uses of atomic energy. Clause 3 of that agreement reads as follows:
It being the intention of the contracting parties to avail themselves, as soon as practicable, of the safeguard facilities created by the international atomic energy agency, the contracting parties may, in respect of this agreement, request the said agency to apply, in such respects and to such extent as the contracting parties may from time to time agree, safeguards in accordance with article XII of the statute of the said agency. Consultations looking to such agreement shall take place upon the request of either contracting party.
My question is: In view of the great dangers from the disposal of atomic wastes in the oceans of the world and in other places, can the minister inform the committee what check the government of Canada makes with respect to clause 3 of this agreement? Does our atomic energy board advise the government as to the safeguards that are required and check to see that the agreement is being kept in that respect?
Matters affecting health or that may affect health in Canada come under the supervision of the atomic energy control board.

I am referring to the disposal of wastes as a result of the use of this uranium in Japan. This article provides for certain safeguards and I am wondering
6158	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce how Canada would check and who advised the government with respect to the application of this clause.

The safeguards that are introduced into these agreements are to make certain that the material will not be used for military purposes. When a country using this uranium for peaceful purposes has a problem, just as we have in Canada or in the United States or in the United Kingdom, with regard to the disposal of waste products that is their own special problem because the people affected are their own people.

I should like to ask the minister to deal with two questions I asked earlier. Has any other province than Ontario shown any interest in co-operating with the federal government in the construction of a nuclear power plant? Second, are there any negotiations under the Japanese-Canadian treaty for the actual sale of uranium to Japan? I understand that the treaty is really just an enabling treaty.

All provinces are aware of the development going on at Chalk River. They are all kept informed and they have representatives in attendance from time to time to consult with the authorities of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and with our scientists at Chalk River so that they know what is ahead in the way of the development of these power reactors. But at the present time, for the erection and use of CANDU, Ontario is the only province which is in a position to take advantage of that development and in a position to pay for it at the time. The amount of electric power that will be produced by CANDU could only be utilized by a grid system as large as the present one in Ontario.
With regard to the bilateral agreement with Japan, it does not require Japan to purchase any given quantity of uranium but it does provide a method by which the sale of uranium to Japan may be made. In the case of countries who have no bilateral agreements sales can be made through private agencies provided they are limited. Where ^ there is a bilateral agreement there is no limitation provided the safeguards are utilized.
Are any negotiations going on under the bilateral treaty at present for the actual sale of uranium to Japan.
My information is that there are some negotiations going on for the sale of Canadian uranium to Japan.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister inform us if any consideration has been given to the matter of co-operation with the United Kingdom? I think the minister questioned my statement that there had been some discussion of this question but the Financial Post points out that the United Kingdom is in a serious position in this field because of the lack of power and that it could prove advantageous both to Canada and the United Kingdom if they were to develop jointly an enriched uranium program that probably could be implemented through the building of a dam and power project at Hamilton falls in Labrador. Would the minister and the department take a look at that type of development as opposed to the one the minister has outlined in which we are now engaged? It would seem that we are pretty well putting all our eggs in one basket and concentrating on the development of natural uranium when at not too much cost we might be able to co-operate with the United Kingdom in the development of enriched uranium using this power source to which I have referred.

I think I asked the hon. member if he had any authority for saying that the United Kingdom was prepared to co-operate with Canada in the development of Hamilton falls for the eventual production of enriched uranium. I have heard of this proposal and have read the article to which the hon. member has referred. We are quite prepared to consider any reasonable proposal that is within the financial reach of our country. I understand that the production of enriched uranium is a very expensive process indeed. If the requirements are such that further enriched uranium should be produced and that this could be done in Canada with the co-operation of the United Kingdom we would certainly be interested in considering the proposition, but at the present time I am not sure that it is feasible or that we have the money available, even jointly with the United Kingdom, to embark upon it. Nor am I certain that there is at present a need for the supplies of enriched uranium which would result from that development.

Item agreed to.
NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL 252. Salaries and other expenses, $26,192,170.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a request to the minister in respect of the development of a more suitable substance for treatment of our highways for winter driving. Under existing conditions and with the materials now used car and truck owners are suffering tremendous damage to their

vehicles from rusting. Furthermore, the salt induces rapid deterioration of cement surfaced walks and roadways. With our researchers doing such remarkable work in other fields, would it not be within the realm of possibility that a non-rusting material for use on our roads could be developed?

I will have to draw to the attention of the national research council the suggestion put forward by my hon. friend. I do not think I can answer offhand but it will be directed to them for consideration. I thought that at this time the committee would perhaps like to have a short statement on the national research council.
The Research Council Act gives the national research council very broad powers in the scientific field, setting it up as an agency to assist and promote scientific research throughout the country. The council discharges its responsibilities in three main ways. First, by providing assistance for the graduate schools of Canadian universities from which come the supply of scientists; second, by giving scholarships to graduate students; and, third, in its laboratories where research of national interest not being done elsewhere is carried out.
The national research council's university support has been continuous for forty-two years and has been increasing rapidly through the last few years. Without minimizing the contributions from other sources, it has been the national research council that has provided the main financial support for university scientific research in Canada. The current expansion of the universities together with the need for increased emphasis on science in the western world has made the financial problem of university research very difficult. The challenge to the council is to increase its university support to meet the accelerated requirements for post-graduate scholarships and research grants. The present status of science in the universities is largely due to financial support from the national research council. Recognizing the present need, the government last year increased national research council support to universities by 70 per cent, that is $2.5 million. It is now proposed to provide a further increase of $2 million, that is 33 per cent, for 1959-60, of which $500,000 applies to medical research. This brings the total national research council support for university research in 1959-60 to approximately $8 million.
The laboratories of the national research council carry out fundamental and applied research in science and engineering that is of national importance and also assist and encourage research in Canadian secondary industries. The more research industry does the 66968-9-390
Supply-Trade and Commerce more interested it is in seeking advice and assistance from the national research council. This leads to the non-obvious conclusion that the more research industry does, the greater the need for the national research council laboratories to expand.
Expenditures by industry on scientific research in Canada have increased from less than $5 million before world war II to $130 million in 1957 and $140 million in 1958. This is an encouraging increase but the total amount is still very low and in some industries no research is being carried out in Canada. In some cases the problem is one of awakening an industry to the need for research; in others, a Canadian firm is a branch only and the parent company does all research and development outside Canada. Industrial research in Canada is directed almost entirely towards development which leaves the council laboratories almost alone in the field of basic industrial research.
The laboratories have undergone a steady growth since 1939 when the staff was about 300 until today, in spite of having split off defence research and atomic energy, the staff numbers about 2,400. During this expansion every effort has been made to maintain a steady and effective expansion of the laboratories as manpower considerations permitted. This steady increase is being continued and the present estimates provide for an increase of staff to 2,511 by March 31, 1960. There is nothing spectacular in the estimates for the laboratories.
The highlight of these estimates are as follows: the total increase of $4,141,376 brings the total requirement of the council to $30,133,580. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I contacted the provincial treasurer of the province of Ontario on Monday morning and he had no reason at all to oppose publication of the announcement of these roads. I think I should just read the list of roads off and then I will say a word about the program itself.
The program is as follows: The first road is from Savant Lake south to Ignace, approximately 90 miles. The second road is from Foleyet to Chapleau south, approximately 60 miles. The third road is from Minaki south, approximately 15 miles. With this road there is the condition that they may go further north, subject to my approval in writing. The fourth road is from Nakina northerly, approximately 50 miles. The fifth is from Goldpines to Uchi Lake, approximately 50 miles. The

sixth is from Port Arthur north, approximately 70 miles. The seventh is from Campbell Red Lake mine to H. G. Young mine, approximately 2 miles. I will read the general description of the eighth road to make it clear:
Resources development roads in the northwesterly part of the province: To facilitate the exploration and development of timber, mineral and commercial Ashing resources. The location of these roads will be determined by the provincial minister, subject to the approval in writing of the minister. The decision of the provincial minister will be based on information that will be supplied from a photoraphic and magnetometer survey along with geological reconnaissance to be carried out in the area north of the Canadian National Railways from Nakina westerly to the Manitoba boundary.
The last road, No. 9, is as follows:
Resources development roads in the northerly part of the province: To facilitate the exploration and development of timber, mineral and commercial Ashing resources. The location will be determined by the provincial minister subject to the approval in writing of the minister.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What is the total mileage?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I cannot give
the hon. member the total including the last two roads, because the routes and mileages have not yet been ascertained; but the total mileage for the first seven roads is 335. That does not include the mileage of the ones in the northwesterly part of the province or the ones in the northerly part of the province which are contemplated.
I would like to say a word on the roads to resources program. This is not a new concept. It was first debated in this house in 1911. It was a proposal of the government of the day led by the Right Hon. Mr. Borden, and it was supported by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The original proposal of 1911 was turned down by the Senate, and the next we heard of this proposal was in the province of Ontario in the thirties. It was a very fine idea, first of all, to open up access to mines, and then it was gradually evolved into a program to include all types of roads.
I should like to make this point about the road program in general and its development, as I see it, across Canada. I should like to make very clear to the house that of our over-all expenditure on national de-velpoment, northern development takes only about 10 per cent. I should like to suggest that already dividends have appeared. This summer over 50 oil and gas exploration parties in the north are using over 400 scientists and men in the first stages of the development program. To point out to the house the significance of this to the people of Canada, three years ago oil and gas revenues totalled about $300,000. This last year ending March 31 it was close to $9 million, which was a sizeable increase. Last year it was $900,000, 66968-9-390i
Supply-Northern Affairs and that is a tenfold increase in one year. If our experience in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon is the same as in Alberta, we can expect eventual revenues of between $100 million and $250 million a year from this source.
I noticed in the discussion here on Saturday that it was mentioned that road costs have been revised upwards. This is true. I could give the committee an example of one road which was mentioned in the debate, the Flat Creek-Eagle Plain road. On the advice of men who helped to build the Alaska highway and who had built roads in the territories, both public and private, I told the committee on mines, forests and waters last year that I expected this first section of the road to cost between $5 million and $8 million. The estimates now are that it will be over $10 million. But when I told the committee that the estimated amount of money which would be spent by the oil and gas companies along the route, mostly on this road but to a lesser degree on roads to the south, will total in the next few years some $200 million, the proportion of money being put into this program by the government as compared with private enterprise is small indeed. I think there is a good example of how you can trigger off expenditures of private enterprise in opening up our resources.
Finally, the purpose of the roads to resources is to open up new country. It is not a winter works proposal. Forest access roads may be. It was designed as one of the first proposals we put forward on winter works, but the roads to resources program is a program of opening up virgin resource areas. The way it works is simple. The province makes the proposals to the federal government and we examine these proposals to see if the criteria we have set up are met. That is to say, whether they open up resources of timber, fish, minerals, tourist wealth and so on. In the case of the province of Nova Scotia and the province of Prince Edward Island where they have not virgin resource areas to open up, we allow them to use roads and open up areas for the tourist industry. This last provision also applies to a small degree to the province of New Brunswick.
I believe, and I believe almost all Canadians will support me in this, that this is a good type of program and it is worthy of support, and if ever a program was evolved with less politics in it or suggestion of politics I would like to know, because I do not think any government, Liberal, Social Credit, C.C.F. or Conservative have intimated in any way to the federal government that these roads should be used for political purposes. These roads are built in areas where there are very

Supply-Northern Affairs few people. The roads that serve the settled areas of our provinces are purely a provincial responsibility, and this is an innovation only in the sense that the federal government has come into the provincial arena of road building in those areas where you want to open up new resources.
Many people over the years have spoken in favour of these access roads or, as we now call them, roads to resources. It is a policy which, I think, is for the good of the country and quite frankly I do not think the program was helped too much by the suggestions that were made here on Saturday. As far as I am concerned I hope hon. members will support me in what I am trying to do to persuade the provinces to help their own future by opening up areas which will benefit from these access roads and, in the west, giving me access, as minister in charge of this department, to the north. That is the theory and the substance of the roads to resources program, and that is how it works.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister has seen fit to criticize the attitude taken by the opposition in this house the other night. We on this side have been very patient with the minister and, of course, we should be because of his inexperience in parliamentary affairs, but I think the time has now come to ask him why it is necessary for the federal government to get permission from the government of Ontario by telephone before the minister can give information to this house as to how a federal appropriation is being spent or, indeed, as is likely, has been spent. Perhaps that is the first question the minister would like to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think that is a reasonable question, and one that the committee should be informed about. In the first instance, when you are working out a roads program with the province there is a good deal of discussion and negotiation which goes on about various roads. I think hon. members here are experienced enough to know that if word gets out in an area of any province, regardless of the politics of that province, that there is a possibility of a road starting from a town and heading north, naturally the people of that town are strongly in support of it. It is also obvious that the people in other districts would like to put forward arguments that their town should be the starting point.
This choice of starting place is purely a provincial responsibility. We are not very much concerned about the starting place of the road. We are concerned that it should open up resources. But if this became a matter of public discussion, the province, no

matter what its political complexion, would be subjected to such pressures that it would become very difficult for the two governments to work out a program bearing in mind only the resource development of this country. I would like to pay a compliment to the governments across this country for maintaining silence while these roads were being negotiated. Even though there were differences between the two governments on points of detail as to what resources were going to be opened up and whether or not it was worth while, these discussions were carried on in a most harmonious fashion. Looking back over the last year and a half of negotiations I can say that my department, the officials particularly, have a right to be proud that all these negotiations were carried on without any acrimony between the governments concerned.
To keep this thing at this level, the government in each case exchanged letters agreeing that there should be no discussion on which roads were being decided upon until an agreement had been completed. In fact, the letter said, until an agreement was signed. In the last five or six months we have been discussing what might be called legal points. Some of the roads have been decided upon in most cases for months, but the legal points of the agreements are still under consideration. That is the reason why there has been this long delay in making announcements.
I think hon. members will appreciate that if I had my way, from my point of view, I would have liked nothing better than to be able to announce progress of this program as the roads were decided upon between ourselves and provincial governments, and not wait until all the legal work was completed. But that was the agreement we made, and that was the agreement I kept to. And as far as the legality of the vote was concerned, I think that the vote last year contained the words "roads that will be built and may be built", and we got authority from that; and this year the words "may be" are left out because I am positive that all the agreements will have been signed within a month or so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this has been a pious explanation, but if I can be impious I should like to say that the minister's explanation is satisfactory except that it does not cover this point: the minister has known for some time that one party to the agreement, in the particular case with which I am concerned the province of Ontario, has been releasing details all along the line. We watched Premier Frost for 18 minutes on television one pre-election night while he was extolling his government for carrying

out this access road program in Ontario, and all the roads to which the minister has referred were mentioned. We heard all about this magnificent road he was building between Savant Lake and Ignace, and how this was going to open up the centre of the northwestern Ontario area. We were told about this marvellous road from Nakina to the Anoconda property which would provide access to the iron ore deposits, and we even got the details about this road from Port Arthur, part of the cost of which would be borne by the Abitibi company and part by the provincial government.
The point which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister-and I do not think it was answered directly, though I think it deserves an explanation-is that if someone is breaking an agreement hon. members of this house should have some protection. I think that is a modest request, and if the minister suggests to us that the province of Ontario and the representatives of northwestern Ontario have not made political hay out of this particular program, then he is naive. Maybe he is naive-I hear that he is-but the hon. gentleman is very naive if he is unaware that political capital has been made out of these projects.
After all, this is what the Frost government fought the election on. The minister may make the excuse that there are not very many people up there, but Premier Frost has made a good deal of play with the vision passed on to him by the Prime Minister. People like the idea that we are booming, and they like the idea that we are developing the north country. This is a good program, on the whole, and some of these roads are good, though there are a couple about which I am doubtful. But for the minister to refuse to give the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and other hon. members here information month after month while all the time the provincial people were making political capital out of it was just unfair to members of parliament. After all, we have some interest in this thing. Perhaps if we had a Conservative member in northwestern Ontario we would have been given this information by the government, but it just happens that northwestern Ontario is a bloc which has no Conservative representation in this house. I am very suspicious that despite the minister's assurances he has been not so much naive as willing to play along the party line in order to support his provincial confrere.
I have said enough about this, but I should like to know the purpose of the road from Goldpines to Uchi Lake and the reason why the province wants to put in that particular
Supply-Northern Affairs road. I want to know why the province wants to put in that road. What are the arrangements with Abitibi on sharing the cost of the road from Port Arthur? I should also very much like to know if any of the roads listed under 9 and 10 are going to go into the area west of Wren lake which is suffering from a budworm epidemic at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Port Arthur has referred to the fact which I think should be noticeable by now that no minister to my knowledge has so postponed the giving of information to which any hon. member of the committee is entitled as has the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The hon. member referred to questions I raised last session about roads to resources in Ontario. Hon. members will recall that there was a delay in answering starred questions and they were carried over for months. No other minister followed such a course. I do not want to be a bad boy in this respect and I know the minister has some obligations to perform and I want him to be able to perform his duties. On the other hand because of his conduct in the last two years with respect to members from northern Ontario he has not deserved any consideration when he is in the jam he is in tonight.
The record speaks for itself. Ignoring last session altogether, if one looks at page 5648 of Hansard, for this session, the appendix that was prepared by the Secretary of State showing unfulfilled requisitions which are normal requisitions-things which I think anyone on the government side would admit were within the competence of any member of parliament to ask-he will observe that there are more items unanswered for which the minister is responsible than there are items with respect to any other department.
I think there is something wrong on the part of the minister in his attempt to ignore requests from an area that has a natural interest in these matters. On three different occasions during the 1958 session I asked the minister questions about a road with which he is perfectly familiar, the prospective road from Kenora to Minaki. On every possible opportunity the minister avoided a direct reply. I want to inform my colleagues in this committee on both sides of the chamber who know something about these things and are, I think, sympathetic, that in 1957 a road was started from Kenora to Minaki for election purposes and the day after the Conservative candidate was defeated work was stopped on that road. The very same thing happened in 1958. I believe the minister owes us an explanation. If we were participating ia

Supply-Northern Affairs politics in days gone by that would perhaps be a typical and natural way of doing things at the time but I want to tell the minister he is 25 or 50 years out of date and this issue is registering in the county.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the minister goes into detail about this, may I say there is a question of principle involved here which is far more than a refusal on the part of the minister to answer questions asked by the hon. members for Port Arthur and Kenora-Rainy River. The House of Commons votes the money for this program. This program has been going on for two years without these agreements being concluded in a formal legal sense with any province except British Columbia. The money has been voted and a good deal of it has been spent.
The minister had the effrontery the other day to suggest that it was McCarthyism for us, who have to vote the money, to ask for information about it. And then in a last minute effort to get his estimates through he said he would telephone the premier of a province to see if the premier would give his consent to his telling the sovereign parliament of Canada what it has a perfect right to know without the consent of any provincial premier.


Now, that is the real point. I say it is not good enough just to give these projects for Ontario.
The hon. member for Timiskaming the other afternoon was very reasonable about this matter. He said if there were some of these roads or routes that had not been agreed upon between any provincial government and the federal government he would not press the minister about those. That is a reasonable attitude because some would not have been agreed upon and might have to be changed. But the hon. member felt we were entitled-and I contend that the House of Commons is entitled-to be told about all those roads concerning which there is no difference of opinion any longer between the provinces and the federal government. Any private arrangement that the minister made with a provincial government to keep this information secret from parliament should not be binding in any way. The minister should either get himself out of such an agreement or parliament should not vote the money. That is the situation.
We should not be voting this money blindly with provincial premiers and provincial ministers of highways going around the country exploiting the grants for political purposes, or even not exploiting for political purposes. Whenever we vote money, except possibly in a few cases to the Department of National Defence, we are entitled to be told what the money is going to be used for before we vote it. It seems to me there is a question of principle here and the minister should do what he has done in the case of Ontario. Of course, there can be no difficulty in British Columbia because the agreement is signed. He should get up and give us the name and description of all these routes in the other provinces about which there is no longer any dispute between the provincial government and the government of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is Tammany hall.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel there is a very important principle involved in this point that has just been raised. It seems to me that the matter of highways comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces, not of this parliament, and where money is voted by this parliament to build highways in any province, then it should be a matter under the jurisdiction of the government of that province to decide just how those highways will be built, when they will be built and where. It also seems to me as a corollary to that, if any announcement is to be made in regard to a highway being built in any province, that announcement should be made by the minister of highways in that province or

certainly, if in this house, only with the consent of that province. As far as I am concerned, in Nova Scotia we feel that highways is a matter that comes under the jurisdiction of our local government, and personally I would think it would be a breach of our provincial autonomy if the minister rose in this house and gave information about the building of a highway in the province of Nova Scotia without the agreement of the government of Nova Scotia. answer I stated quite candidly that I could not see there was any reason whatever of a political nature-there was no election in the offing-for not giving this information and immediately this stampede starts.
