maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter is of such importance from the point of view of the rights of this parliament that I am sure the matter cannot be allowed to rest with the statements that have been made thus far by hon. members. I believe there is a duty on each member of this house, no matter where he sits, to address himself to the right of parliament in respect of a proposal made by the government for moneys for a particular purpose, to insist on the right to know all the circumstances connected with that request.
I have before me the observations of the leader of the opposition in 1938, the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett, who stated what I think is not only a matter of privilege for members of this house, but what at the same time involves a duty in the case of any member who feels a particular situation needs elucidation, particularly a matter that has to do with a proposal by a minister for the expenditure of public money. Mr. Bennett, at page 3834 of Hansard tor 1938, volume 4, said the following:
One of the duties of that branch of the House of Commons known as the opposition is to investigate the expenditure of public moneys. Unfortunately the present opposition is small in numbers, so there falls upon me a much larger obligation than I like to contemplate, but one which as long as I occupy this position and am paid a salary for it under the provisions of the Public Service Act I shall continue to discharge to the best of my ability.
That statement surely justifies the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition and others in the remarks they have made this evening, and some of the remarks that were made by some other hon. members in this committee on Saturday last. Mr. Bennett goes on and at the same page he said:
When public finance is involved it is the duty of every member of the opposition to endeavour to show whether the country got the greatest value possible for its money.
How can that possibly be done unless we are given all of the information, information which the minister, mistaking his function, I believe, felt on Saturday and apparently

feels tonight he cannot properly and completely give to the house? This is surely a matter going to the very roots of this institution which we call a free parliament. If there can be any doubt about the words of Mr. Bennett I would refer the house to the commentary in that authorative book by Professor Dawson entitled, "The Government of Canada". At page 439 Professor Dawson says:
Inasmuch as virtually all government activities entail expenditures, and as most of these expenditures must be authorized by the approval of estimates, it follows that sooner or later the house must pass on most of these activities of the government in committee of supply. Each item-
I ask the minister to pay attention to these words; I ask the minister who is leading the house to pay attention to these words, because these are the kind of words we were reminded about when hon. gentlemen sat on this side and said that the former administration continuously disregarded the rights of parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask what page that is?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Page 439. I will read it again because I do not believe that the two ministers associated with this particular matter at this time were free to appreciate the full implications of what I had begun to read.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Dispense.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Someone says "dispense". That is typical of the attitude of the government as now constituted. They do not want to be reminded of our obligations to parliament. Dispense with reminding us. Dispense with calling in an authority that will establish the necessity of the government observing the well-known traditions of parliament, traditions which the Prime Minister hopes at some time or other to embody in a memorable document that will enshrine the rights of free citizens in this country. Dispense! This government is one of those governments in the history of Canada that requires to be reminded continually of the obligation of the government to the people and to parliament itself. Professor Dawson wrote on page 439:
Inasmuch as virtually all government activities entail expenditures, and as most of these expenditures must be authorized by the approval of estimates, it follows that sooner or later the house must pass on most of these activities of the government in committee of supply.
Then he goes on:
Each item in the estimates is debatable-
Each item. How can each item be debatable if the minister refuses to give us information on which to base an argument for debate?

Each item of the estimates is debatable, and any member may move to have it reduced or struck out.
Then he quotes Mr. Bennett:
"When public finance is involved it is the duty of every member of the opposition to endeavour to show whether the country got the greatest value possible for its money."
How can we possibly do that? How can that duty possibly be discharged unless we are given the right of scrutinizing to the fullest extent in accordance with the wishes of any particular member? The minister says, in exercising his best judgment, this is something he could not do. We shall analyse the reasons for that in a few moments. Then the author goes on to say:
Members may demand information in great detail, and can hold up the estimates until the desired material is produced. Thus . . . Mr. M. J. Cold-well, the C.C.F. leader, has stated the position of the private member in strong but not exaggerated terms.
These are the words of Mr. Coldwell.
"There is one place and one place only in this parliament where private members are supreme, namely, in supply when discussing the estimates. This is His Majesty's purse, and the age old right of members of parliament is to decide to what extent His Majesty's purse shall be filled. That is what we are doing now, and I certainly wish to protest against any precedent being established that would curtail the right of this parliament to discuss any matters in connection with the administration of the minister's department."
Surely if hon. gentlemen have forgotten this principle this recital from Mr. Bennett, a distinguished Conservative prime minister-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am glad hon. members applauded. I hope they will applaud and pay tribute to his memory by observing the precepts of parliamentary practice which he laid down. If these words are truly representative of the concepts applicable to this deliberative assembly, surely the minister was in error on Saturday last when he refused to give information which he said he was honour bound not to disclose to this house because of an agreement that he had made with the premier of Ontario.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Or with any other premier.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Or with any other premier. Surely if such an agreement was made the minister must recognize by this time how invalid and improper such an agreement was. The minister could have said to Premier Frost, "I will do my best not to add to your own particular difficulties but I can go no farther than that. I must tell you, Mr. Premier, that if any member of the House of Commons asks me for information as to what is to be done with moneys that I am 66968-9-391
Supply-Northern Affairs asking parliament to vote I will have no alternative, indeed, I have the duty to tell parliament why I am asking for moneys in this particular instance."
Surely that is the correct situation. I felt rather concerned tonight when I realized the position in which the minister found himself, and I am sure that the house, generous as it always is, fully appreciates the situation confronting the minister in respect of other obligations. But we have a duty to perform. The minister came to the house tonight and gave no evidence whatsoever of appreciation of the elementary principle involved in refusing parliament this information.
First of all, he criticized parliament for its conduct on Saturday. He began his statement by saying that he had spoken over the telephone to the provincial treasurer of Ontario and as a result of having had that telephone conversation, not with the head of the government of Ontario but with the provincial treasurer who, by the way, comes from northern Ontario where some of these roads are, he tells us as a minister of this government that he has received from an Ontario minister his consent to give the parliament of Canada some of the particulars behind a matter involving a vote which the House of Commons is asked to consider.
If ever there has been a failure to appreciate the function of this kind of deliberative assembly, surely we have had it tonight. I am not commenting on the merits of the proposal. Undoubtedly this program has much to commend it. But there can be no justification for not giving the information in the absence of a decision of parliament itself either not to ask for the information or to accept that there are special reasons why it should not be given. First of all, the minister did not even explain that there were difficulties in the way of his acceding readily to what undoubtedly he would have had to admit he must do. This was not done. He simply said, I cannot do this; I am in honour bound not to do it. I have an agreement with the heads of provincial governments and I respect my agreement with provincial governments, he might as well have gone on to say, more than I respect the rights and privileges of this free parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Someone says "nonsense", and that is typical of the penetrating, pregnant answer we receive from government benches when they find themselves in an embarrassing position as they obviously do at this very moment.
The reason why we must insist on this is because, as in 1938 when Mr. Bennett spoke
6168	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs as leader of the opposition, leading a small group, he had to realize that there might be other similar situations confronting parliament. He wanted to see that the principles which he fully recognized as sacrosanct would be observed. This is exactly the position we must take tonight, so that no other minister of this government on some other occasion will come in here and say, I cannot give this information because I have made an arrangement with some provincial premier.
I am not discussing this matter from the point of view of its connection with circumstances which led to members of a provincial parliament, in the course of an election, being given information which is being denied to the members of this house. I am not placing my case on that ground. I am placing my case on the elementary principle that a minister must fully answer any question put to him from any section of the house; that is elementary.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? In view of what the hon. gentleman is saying, is it the policy of his party that the details of every sort of financial grant to all the provinces be carefully examined and controlled by this house?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have stated that it is the duty of any minister, I do not care to what party he belongs, in a parliament such as this to disclose information which is asked by any hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Answer the question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is not satisfied, he can get up after I have finished my statement-
Some hon Members: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-and he can give us this new concept of a bill of rights if he wishes.
I want to say this; so long as I am in this house no member of the government is going to say to me that I am not entitled, as a representative of a part of the people of this country and with a wider responsibility like other members to all the people in this country, to elicit from the government the kind of details which will enable me to decide whether a request made for further moneys should be approved. That is an elementary principle. Let there be no doubt about this: the right hon. gentleman who now leads this government had no hesitation in affirming this principle when, as in so many places, on April 26 he said:
Parliament has been treated with shocking contempt, sorely wounded and robbed of its rights.
I say not only has the minister treated parliament with shocking contempt, sorely


wounded it and robbed it of its rights, but the hon. gentlemen who sit behind him, by their support of him in this particular
instance are guilty of the same breach of the rights of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to say to the committee that after listening to the hon. member for Essex East intoning unctuously, with all the pomposity at his command about the rights of parliament, I am very pleased indeed to find that after twenty-two years in the government and two years in the opposition he has finally learned to appreciate the fundamental principles which he read to us just a moment ago. I think that all people who are interested in results in this country will recognize that these roads to resources agreements to be concluded are presently under negotiation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not what you said the other night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Quebec is excluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The province of British Columbia has signed an agreement. Eight other provinces have agreements under negotiation. I made it very clear to the committee that in the interest of developing resources instead of developing votes-which is the only thing the opposition knows about -we agreed, not in any personal deal between myself and the other governments but as a matter of ethics between sovereign administrations in this country. The Leader of the Opposition, with no experience in domestic matters-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -stands up in this house-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: How many elections did you lose?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
These interruptions from hon. gentlemen opposite show how unaccustomed they are, after years of living in idleness on the back benches of this house, to being on the other side of the house.
I was just saying a word about the Leader of the Opposition. He was good enough to say I was inexperienced in my task. I would say that is, to a large extent, true. I am doing my level best to learn my job and do it well. I hope that the Leader of the Opposition will also grow in stature as a leader of the opposition knowledgeable in domestic affairs. If he goes back and remembers his own statements made over the years, some of the things he has held up as examples of how negotiations should be carried on between governments; if he would recall the number of times when as secretary of state for external affairs he condemned secret

diplomacy but stressed the importance of secrecy when negotiations were being conducted, he would not say, I think, that the public should have all the information and that parliament should have all the information, while negotiations were under way. However, these are phrases he will remember: negotiations should not be prejudiced by the spotlight of publicity. Now, he asks me as the minister of a department to break these very tenets that he has espoused. He asks me while negotiations are going on with eight of the nine provinces to divulge every little detail.
I tried to be helpful to the committee in the case of Ontario. Last week the provincial authorities in Ontario finally met, so far as we were concerned in the department, all the proposals that we had put forward in connection with this agreement from a legal standpoint. It was for this reason I was ready on Saturday, in the interest of cooperation with members of the C.C.F. party who were raising these questions, to give them the information they asked, knowing that the negotiations at least at the department level for the province of Ontario were now concluded. They are still not through the cabinet yet.
In the case of Manitoba only today did we receive an answer to the last letter I wrote debating one of the terms in the agreement. The letter has come in although I have not actually seen it myself. I still am a little concerned over my own actions in agreeing to give this information on Ontario. I felt honestly bound to give that information to the committee, because I believe as strongly as I can that this committee has a right to all the information it can get on the spending of money by this parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Just the information we can get?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This information that I would like to provide would be as detailed as it comes in to me. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond suggested the opposition was asking the government to go a bit far into the affairs of a province than is ordinarily expected. It may be all right for a government that believes in centralization and taking over control of a province and eventually the municipalities; but I do not think there are serious minded members of this house who would say about the trans-Canada agreement, for instance, that before the money is voted each year every detail of every contract in every province must be laid before this house. I would suggest that hon. members would have the right to ask for all this information as soon as it was available, but if they held 66968-9-391i
Supply-Northern Affairs up their votes until the province had completed all its arrangements for the whole year it would be impossible in practice to get the trans-Canada highway built.
This program is clear. I gave to the committee in the estimates last year a clear outline of this program. For each province there is a maximum of $15 million. Last year I told the house there was a term of five years. This year I told the house that starting last fall we had changed the firm commitment of a five-year limit and made a term in each agreement suitable to the province concerned. The agreements vary from five to eleven years.
I have made this information clear, but I would like to put forward this proposition, that the province has the right to choose the location of the roads and has the right to let the contracts. We are expected to protect the spending of public money, and we have the right to examine and see if those roads meet the criteria parliament accepted last year when first voting this item, namely whether they open up resources. We also have the right to examine and see if the money is well spent. Personally, if I were a provincial cabinet minister I would resent any federal government, which was making, in effect, a conditional grant, coming in and saying, "We want all the information before you spend a dollar and before we vote the money." As I say, we have the right as the federal government to make certain that before the federal government pays any money we have looked into it to see that the money will be well spent.
I told the house on Saturday that with one exception no money has been spent under this vote because no agreement has been signed. The exception is British Columbia. I do not know how much more I would have to say, Mr. Chairman, to make it clear to hon. members that this program is a good program. I have had tremendous co-operation from all the provinces in working it out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What about Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think as the years roll by it will rank as one of the most imaginative and constructive proposals ever put forward by a federal government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What about Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have the temerity to believe that as these roads are built and new resource areas open up the new wealth discovered will more than make up for any money we put into these roads. I think also as the years go on and we try to assess this roads program in relation to other great projects in Canada's history, this roads to resources concept, first put forward

Supply-Northern Affairs in this house in 1911 and brought into effect in 1958, will rank with the significance of the Canadian Pacific railway.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I will not detain the committee very long at this point. The minister, speaking from the depths of his experience as an elder statesman, has been good enough to wish me well and to hope that I will grow in stature. Perhaps eventually I may be successful in reaching his heights, but I quite admit I have not got the minister's broad and deep experience in these matters, that is true. He has been working on roads now for a couple of years and ought to know something about them, but apparently he has not learned in two years the difference between the trans-Canada highway which is built, as far as federal government participation is concerned, through a statutory grant, and these highways which are in appropriations each year as part of the minister's department. But no doubt the minister will pick up these details as he goes along and eventually he may learn something about diplomacy.
I was not sure when the minister first spoke whether he was condemning secret diplomacy or open diplomacy. He reminded me of the number of times I had condemned secret diplomacy at the United Nations. That is what I am condemning now, secret diplomacy between the government of Ontario and the minister, so secret that while the premier of Ontario can tell everything over television, no member of this House of Commons can find out from the minister how this federal money is to be spent, or at least, he admits in one case has been spent.
Then the minister said, "No agreements have been made, so how can you expect me to talk about these things before an agreement had been made?" The minister said on page 5883 of Hansard for July 11:
I can say this, that in Ontario there are seven roads upon which agreements have been made.
The minister is getting into his usual difficulty of saying one thing on one occasion and something else on another occasion, and when we point that out he accuses us of inexperience or quibbling with words.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Or McCarthyism.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Or McCarthyism. The minister said the other night that there were seven agreements about roads, but we will not know about them because he said at the same time, "As long as I keep my share of the bargain, I feel my conscience is clear;" no matter what the premier of Ontario may do during an election period, he does not


want to do anything after an election period. Every time the minister speaks on these matters he gets himself in more deeply, and I would advise him to say as little as possible if he wants to get his estimates through in time to get to Saskatchewan.
Then the minister said, repeating what has been said by an hon. member, "We would be prejudicing provincial rights if we got this information in the house." There is going to be spent $9 million of federal money. I think he said, "We would be going a bit far and prejudicing provincial rights." That is a strange doctrine of provincial rights and federal authority that a member of this parliament is not to be told by the minister how the money that this parliament is being asked to vote is to be spent, or in one case has been spent, and no amount of unctuous sophistry on the part of the minister will explain away the fact that last Saturday he refused to give this committee the information to which it was entitled. The reason he gave us was that we should not really worry about it because the election was over. The election in Ontario was over; why should we want to know about it any more? Then the minister gets up tonight and says twice that there is no politics in this matter; "I am doing my duty as well as I can."

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I ask the
hon. Leader of the Opposition, if we had announced these roads before the election would he have complained then?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am sorry, would you repeat that?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was just
suggesting that if the government of Ontario had announced these roads before the election-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: They did.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-the hon.
member would have some reason to complain.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister must know, because he was politically interested in this election, that every night during the provincial election, before the election, information was being given by the candidates from northern Ontario about these roads. It was being used for election purposes. Candidates could do that over the air, but a member of parliament could not get that information in this house even after the election.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The thing that bothers me about the minister's replies and which, I should like to suggest, amounts to evasion, is this: he knows that I came to him many months ago in this house and told him and

his executive assistant that these representatives were announcing these roads in our region, that details were being given, and that in one case even the contractor who was going to get the job was being named. I felt it was unfair because we could not get that information and the minister agreed to give me the information in confidence.
But my point is this: why should someone on the other side of the agreement be able to go around blatting it all over the place while members of parliament should have to keep silent?. I might say that the provincial government has taken all of the credit for this project. Why, the minister is not even known as a visionary up in northern Ontario. It is all Old Man Ontario and his good friends George and Clare. I should like to think that the minister and the government might get a bit of credit for this, but no. All the credit is going to Old Man Ontario. I should like to think that this deal with Ontario is being worked out in equal partnership, but it seems to me that, as in some of the divorce cases, one partner is pure and above reproach and the other is going around committing adultery all over the place.
We have an example here which I hope the minister will not follow in the future. If any evidence comes forward that someone is not keeping the agreement, I think we deserve to have the information here and I think the minister should give us that assurance before we go any further into this topic and into the detail. I think he should give us an assurance that in future we should have this information as soon as one scrap of it is revealed by the other party. I, certainly, could have provided the minister with concrete proof if he had wanted it, but I would have assumed he would take my word for it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not want this discussion to be confined to the province of Ontario. I make a request to the minister that he should give to this committee, and give to the committee now, the names of all the roads in the eight provinces with regard to which agreement in principle had been reached. Otherwise we shall be asked to vote this money blind wtihout even knowing how it is to be used. It will be a blank cheque to the minister, and he will be able to change this around in any way he likes. I should also like to ask the minister if he would tell us how much of the $9 million voted last year was spent in each province and for what projects in each province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
When I heard the hon.
member for Essex East making the argument he did I was able to understand the fear which some people have regarding invasions
Supply-Northern Affairs of provincial autonomy. What the hon. member said was that when money is granted to a province, this federal parliament has the right to examine in detail how that money is spent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
So far as the
federal account is concerned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
These funds are granted in respect to roads to be built by the provinces, and only the provincial government has the right to decide how the money is to be spent. As far as this house is concerned, I do not think that under our constitutional system we are entitled to discuss anything other than whether or not the grant has actually been made to the province. If we were to adopt the principle advanced by the hon. member for Essex East it would mean that every grant made to a provincial government in respect of education, hospitals or for any other purpose could be debated as to the detailed expenditure in this chamber. We have the right to question expenditures, but the expenditure here before us concerns only the writing of a cheque to a provincial government. The details of how that money is spent are a matter for that government. I say, further, that the only right we have in regard to that money is as provided under the agreement with the province to whom the money is passed over.
In this case, where an agreement is made for the building of highways according to certain specifications, this house has the right to see to it that the agreement is kept, but we have no right to say where a road will go or anything of that nature, and certainly in a case such as the present one I do not think constitutionally we have the right to ask the minister of northern affairs to give out information except that which he is entitled to give under the agreement, and under the terms of the agreement in this case he has quite properly checked with the provincial government concerned before he has released information.
If we were to say anything else in this committee, the detailed expenditure of every cent we gave to a province from now on would be a matter which could be debated in this chamber even though the money had been spent by the province for matters within provincial jurisdiction only and our part had only been to make a grant.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I ask the minister
whether he agrees with this doctrine of federal-provincial financial relationship which has just been expounded by the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
He is asking you.

Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the Leader
of the Opposition had been listening a moment ago he would have heard me lay down what I thought. In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with regard to the money spent in each province of the $9 million voted last year, the information is as follows: British Columbia, $1,000,732.39; Saskatchewan, $750,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is all that was spent. And were there agreements with these two provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There was an agreement with British Columbia since November 4, 1958. No agreement was signed with the province of Saskatchewan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In other words, the minister is telling us that money was spent in Saskatchewan without there being any agreement whatsoever.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That point was raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West on Saturday and I was about to remind the hon. member for Ottawa West that this matter was fully explained in the standing committee on mines, forests and waters as reported on page 951 of the proceedings in evidence No. 32 for June 5, 1959.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Will the minister read the explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes. If the committee does not object I will read from this statement because there was a series of questions and answers in the evidence. I might just add that the payment for Saskatchewan was made in February of 1959 and was charged to appropriations for 1958-59 and not to the estimates which are now before the house, those for 1959-60. In last year's estimates, a vote similar to item 280 appeared as item 289, but there was one significant difference in this wording from the wording of the vote this year. It referred to contributions "in accordance with agreements that have been or may be entered into by Canada and the provinces."
The explanation is as follows:
Saskatchewan was one of the first provinces to get work under way on the roads to resources program. Before the end of the fiscal year 1958-59 the government of Saskatchewan represented to us that they had made very substantial expenditures and had recovered no money from the federal government, with the result that the province was suffering financial hardship. Saskatchewan had been ready to sign the formal agreement, but the decision to make the construction schedule more flexible had caused some delay. In the circumstances, the government of Saskatchewan asked that a payment might be made covering somewhat less than half the money the province had already spent on the program.

Even though the wording of the vote referred to agreements that have been or may be entered into between Canada and the provinces, I consulted with my own legal officers and asked them to take the matter up with the solicitor to the treasury to make sure beyond doubt of the propriety of such a payment. After careful consideration it was the concensus of the various legal officers that no payment should be charged to the vote unless an agreement had been entered into but that the agreement need not necessarily be of a formal nature. There was no question but that we had reached agreement with the province of Saskatchewan, which was embodied in the exchange of letters between the two governments. I therefore made a submission to the treasury board in which I stated that agreement had been reached through correspondence with the province of Saskatchewan on the roads to be constructed under the roads to resources program, the standards and specifications to which they are to be built, and the terms and conditions governing Canada's contribution to the province in respect to the cost of constructing such roads. In these circumstances I recommended that I be given authority to make a payment in the amount of $750,000 to the province of Saskatchewan. This recommendation was approved by treasury board on February 5, 1959 under authority of treasury board minute 544145 and a cheque for $750,000 was sent to the province the same day.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that this explanation will make it clear to the hon. member that there was no impropriety in making that payment to the province of Saskatchewan. As I said before, we have a formal agreement signed with British Columbia and there is no necessity to explain that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister two factual questions. First, will he tell us what was the road in Saskatchewan to which this matter referred? Second, will he tell us whether or not the agreement with British Columbia requires federal auditing of the expenditures before the money is paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the agreement with British Columbia is that the provincial auditors will present these figures and we will accept them on the assumption that the provincial auditor is an accredited business firm.
With respect to the other question, there are three roads in the Saskatchewan roads program. These are the Otosquen road, the Hanson lake road and the Uranium City road. As I understand it they have completed the Otosquen and are working on the Hanson lake road and part of the Uranium City road.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in his
answer about British Columbia I believe the minister has answered completely the fallacious argument of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. In other words the minister says he does not pay out any money under this agreement until he is

satisfied that the money has been spent for the purpose for which parliament voted it. So the extraordinary doctrine we listened to a few moments ago from the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond is not, according to the minister's own evidence, followed by the government which the hon. member was trying to support by his argument.
In the same context, of course, the minister is, I am sure, well aware that no money is paid under the trans-Canada highway arrangements until there has been a proper audit and a very distinguished former member of this house from Nova Scotia withheld the payment in one province for a very considerable time until there was some further investigation into some aspects of the roads program in that province. So there can be no question whatever that parliament has a perfect right to know and the Auditor General in the end has to certify that this money has been properly spent for the purpose for which parliament is voting it.
The purpose the minister is asking us to vote this for is to spend money for roads leading to resources in accordance with agreements entered into between Canada and the provinces. The minister said that a certain sum had already been spent in one province-$250,000 or something like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The sum of
$750,000 in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the only case?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There has been no money spent of the $9 million we are being asked to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not one cent of the present $9 million has been spent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the minister in a position to give us the names of the roads in the other eight provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot, Mr. Chairman. Whenever I have been able to I have done so. I cannot give that information because these agreement have not gone through cabinet yet and in several of the provinces a great deal depends on the negotiations we are carrying on with them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I want to make it clear again that I am only asking about those roads concerning which there is no dispute with the provinces. This was the information asked for the other day by the hon. member for Timiskaming. I can understand the minister's hesitation in giving information concerning roads about which negotiations are in process, but surely if there is complete
Supply-Northern Affairs agreement there cannot be any reason for secrecy, not the faintest reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am informed by my officials who are looking for this information that outside of Saskatchewan and British Columbia there are points of discussion still going on with them all. I understand that ten days ago Ontario came along with its answer to my last letter. I will have to bring this to cabinet and if it is acceptable it will be approved. If these points are under discussion I cannot possibly mention the roads in question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, why did the
minister himself say last Saturday as reported at page 5883 of Hansard:
1 can say this, that in Ontario there are seven roads upon which agreements have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Because, Mr. Chairman, we were that far advanced in Ontario that I felt free to give that information to the committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am very inexperienced in these matters, Mr. Chairman, but an agreement has been made or it has not been made. No matter how far you may be on the road to an agreement there comes a time when you make it and then the agreement is finished in so far as negotiation is concerned. At least, that is the way we conduct affairs internationally. I suppose the minister follows the same pirnciples of negotiation. On Saturday he said that there were seven roads upon which agreements had been made. Have they been made or have they not been made? If they are not yet completed, why did he say they had been made when he spoke on Saturday?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think this is a question of a misunderstanding, Mr. Chairman. In the case of Ontario the negotiations on the actual physical location of the roads and standards are completed but a formal agreement has not yet been signed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister told us the other day-perhaps some one could look it up-that $3 million had been spent on this program in the province of Prince Edward Island. I was astonished at that figure and I must say I am still astonished at it. Can the minister explain it?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In the province of Prince Edward Island the estimated total expenditures up to the end of March 31, 1959, totalled $2,500,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
But the minister said no money was spent of last year's vote except
6174	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs in Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Now he tells us that $2,500,000 was spent in Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I made the mistake of assuming that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was smart enough to realize that it was provincial money that was spent. The federal government has not spent any money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think with the hon.
gentleman's experience this would sound like another vision. We in this committee are not interested in what the provincial government is spending. What the minister said the other day-I could look it up in a moment-was that $3 million had been spent as a part of this program. I expressed the view that $1,500,000 was the maximum for each province. He said that it was, but that the $3 million was the total expenditure of which we were to share half. Now he says these are provincial expenditures. Where does the federal government come into the item at all?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps I should read what the minister said last Saturday on this point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that it is ten o'clock the established time for adjournment. The chairman should ask if it is the desire of the committee to sit beyond the hour. Before he does that perhaps I can express our attitude in that regard and say that this evening there are extremely special circumstances which would warrant proceeding beyond ten o'clock which we think could have been overcome, of course, if the house leader had been able to keep the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources closer to his itinerary. Nevertheless, there are special circumstances which will cause the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to be away tomorrow. Because of that we will be certainly most co-operative in extending the sitting beyond ten o'clock this evening. It is hoped that this will be no indication of any future action.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent to continue?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No. Hon. gentlemen have made no move tonight to get the estimates through. If they want to sit here, I do not.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was going to say that in view of the circumstances which were announced by the acting house leader earlier, and in view of what has been said by the hon. member for Skeena, we on this side of the house would be prepared to


carry on for some time longer in the hope that the desire of the house leader would be accomplished. I cannot assure the committee that that will be so, but I can assure the committee of this. If the minister will show more co-operation in connection with the questions that were asked perhaps we could get on much faster.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Will the committee give unanimous consent to continue?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Before we do that I wonder whether I could have any indication from the government or the house leader as to the time? I would suggest at this stage that we sit until eleven o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would it be possible to carry on until we get at least this department through so that the minister will be able to carry on tomorrow where he wishes to be? It will not take all night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps if we leave it wide open like that we will have more cooperation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In a spirit of co-operation I would like to clear up this difficulty about expenditures in Prince Edward Island. A moment ago the minister said there were no such expenditures, but at page 5885 of Hansard the minister is reported as follows:
In Prince Edward Island, 343 miles of road-on that little island-and they spent $2,500,000 last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that they spent $2,500,000 in Prince Edward Island? I thought the limit for each province was $1,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The limit each year in a province is $3 million, of which we pay one-half, $1,500,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And $2,500,000 was spent in Prince Edward Island last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the figure I have here.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, the quotation read by the Leader of the Opposition is absolutely correct. The amount spent by the province of Prince Edward Island was $2,500,000, and it was spent entirely out of provincial funds. If the agreement is signed we will have to pay one-half of that. In no year may there be more than $3 million spent in a province, and therefore our maximum in any one year in any one province is $1,500,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Does the minister mean by that that he is now negotiating with Prince Edward Island about roads that have already

been built and that there is no agreement about those roads, and yet we cannot be told about them?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, we are still negotiating.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Surely, Mr. Chairman, that is more preposterous than anything we have yet been told about this whole preposterous business. Here are those roads that have already been built, that every human being in Prince Edward Island, the whole 100,000, must know about and yet we cannot be told here in this house. It really is beyond anything that we have heard yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In one of his earlier remarks the minister made reference to the fact that he hoped hon. members would help him to persuade the various provincial governments that they should participate in this so-called roads to resources program. I wonder what he means by asking for assistance in helping to persuade provinces to participate; for certainly, in so far as British Columbia is concerned, the agreement has been signed, the road has been established and that is the end of it in so far as federal participation is concerned. That was the indication given by the minister on Saturday last when we were discussing the question of bridges 150 miles from a road, that in so far as British Columbia was concerned it was out of the question because the agreement had been signed. What does he mean by asking members to help him to persuade provincial governments to participate when he has in fact closed the door to any further participation, especially with those provinces that have already signed agreements and almost closed the door with provinces that are on the verge of having signed agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I had a certain amount of difficulty in hearing the hon. member for Skeena but I think I got most of it. The agreement with British Columbia, as the hon. member knows, was signed early in the fall of 1957. Since that time-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Signed when?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
November 4, 1958. I used the wrong year. In that agreement there were no bridges; therefore, I suggested to the hon. member who is questioning me that he should not get too enthusiastic that he was going to get a bridge under the British Columbia agreement because the agreement had already been signed and they had used up their full amount of $15 million, which is the limit of which we can share 50 per cent of under this agreement.
Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister is right in so far as bridges are concerned. The minister said he hoped hon. members here would give their endorsation to the program and assist him in persuading the provincial governments to participate. Which provincial governments need persuading to participate in this program?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There are nine governments in agreement with this program and one that is not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the minister suggesting that hon. members in this house assist him in persuading one government to participate?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On to Quebec!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not know what he means by that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am only suggesting that I am very proud of this agreement. I hope all provinces will eventually be in it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am still not getting anywhere, Mr. Chairman, in my endeavours to protect the dignity and the right of a federal member of parliament to know in relationship to a provincial member of parliament. I told the minister on Saturday that we have an incomparable sunshine blowhard up at the lakehead who every week has some sort of road or road contract to announce. It is a bridge or it is a culvert, or it is some granular base, or road of some kind. And most of the roads that he has been announcing in the last five or six months have been tied in with this particular program.
He has even given to the newspapers the details of a most unusual contract. I want to know about it right now, and it is this arrangement between the provincial government, Abitibi and the federal government for this road to resources out of Port Arthur. I would like to know something about this particular road and why this gentleman is able to make these announcements and we cannot even confirm whether they are right or not. I still feel that the minister has not answered that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On the score of holding me responsible for what is done by provincial M.L.A.'s, I cannot do anything about that. My job is here and that is what I try to do. As for the question about information on the road, I am always glad to oblige if I can do it. There is a clause in the Ontario agreements, for example, which reads as follows:
If the minister approves in writing Ontario may enter into an agreement with a mining, lumber or other resource development company, providing for the construction by the company of a part of the
6178	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs project which will be primarily for the benefit of the company and that the province will pay to the company two-thirds of the cost of construction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could the minister say what document he is reading from?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This is one of
the drafts of one of the agreements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the road being built on a draft?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The road is almost completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I go back and say that over the years there have been precedents established in old agreements whereby the federal government has participated with a province and a private company in regard to these mining access roads. At various times the department, which had other names than northern affairs, used to enter into this type of deal, and I think that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has the same type of program. This J-j-J rule was also made available to the provinces under the roads to resources program and several of the provinces have taken advantage of it. This road from Port Arthur north has that provision. I am informed with respect to that road that the Abitibi company has agreed to pay up to one-third of the cost of the road up to a standard that was agreed upon between the provincial government and Abitibi and the other two-thirds will be paid by the province and ourselves. If the road is built to a higher standard then the additional amount required to build it to that higher standard is paid 50 per cent by the federal government and 50 per cent by the provincial government. I think that is all the information on that road.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I might point out to the minister that when Mr. Ambridge was here several weeks ago he told us about that road. Here is another example where the minister would not give us information. When a road is in a member's constituency I think he is entitled to the information. Here is a case where a private corporation had the information and was revealing it and where the provincial member was also revealing it. The minister says that we cannot hold them responsible. What kind of an agreement is this if you cannot hold the other person responsible for divulging information? It is not an agreement at all. It is a farce. I should like to suggest to the minister that if he is going to have these peculiar three-sided agreements in which the other two sides seem to have all the leeway and he is squeezed right out then it is about time that he had


a talk with these people and tried to remind them that an agreement is an agreement instead of reminding us. ,
I should like to know about the road from Nakina to the Anaconda deposits, whether it is under the same kind of agreement and, if not, why not.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not have very much to add to what I have already said with regard to the point made by the hon. member for Port Arthur. I telephoned the government of Ontario when I heard last fall that there had been this leak and received the assurance of the Ontario government that there had not been any leak from sources close to them, and there was nothing else for me to do but to take that as their attitude on the matter. When they assured me that nothing of that sort was being done and they were honouring their agreement I had no other choice but to accept their statement. Another province apparently made an announcement, the province of Prince Edward Island, and I received many complaints in that regard. I took the same stand as I took in the house, that I could not break what was a signed statement on my part in a letter that there should not be any announcement made until there was common agreement to make an announcement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: All I can say is that the Conservative members in northwestern Ontario made the minister a liar in jig-quick time and repeatedly. In these highway programs where the federal government is paying up to 50 per cent of the cost and where there are programs with agreements with private companies, I think the members from the areas concerned deserve the information. I am not going to labour the point further but I think they deserve the information. I should like to know whether you have another three-sided agreement with respect to the road from Nakina north to the Anaconda deposits and, if not, why not.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As far as we
know in the department there is no definite information as to a third interest. I believe that it is sometimes the policy of the provincial government, if they think a company might be interested in an area, to build a road through that area to encourage their interest, but there is no third party in this agreement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This is a case where I think there should be. I see no reason why Abitibi should be taken for a road that is going to open up resources and Anaconda should not be paying a contribution of some kind although in the case of Anaconda the resource

is in the exploration stage. The Abitibi road and the other roads that are involved bring up the whole question of the relationship of funds of the federal government going to the provinces for forest access roads because in effect, whether you call it a forest access road or a road to a resource it is a forest access road.
The road south from Savant Lake to Ignace also goes across some crown lands held by the provincial government that are under licence to companies. I want to know what is the relationship here. We can get into most uneven and unfair development if certain companies are going to have to put up part of the cost of a road running through or tapping their limits and other companies are going to get these roads without having to make a contribution. What was the idea in mind in this regard in so far as the federal government is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think I can put it this way, that where there is an operation already in effect and a road going in that will be of direct benefit to them there is a J-J-J split but where you are going into a virgin area in the hope of attracting companies to develop that area there is usually a 50-50 split. The discrimination to which the hon. member refers is happening all the time. I have these complaints come to me about the roads we are building in the Northwest Territories. Companies have gone in there in the past and pioneered their own winter roads. They say, "Why did you not come along and build us a road?" The fact is that they were ahead of our development program and they paid the cost. We obviously feel sorry for them, and the companies that come later get all the benefit of the work done by the pioneering companies or by the government in a particular case. But that is the way it works out. You cannot have such a thing as a perfect set-up whereby everything would go in all at once.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to know about the road from Goldpines to Uchi Lake. As I remember that country, it must run through the tentative limit that is going to the Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company. I understand that under the terms of the contract between Anglo-Newfoundland and the provincial government they have undertaken to spend so much money on road and water developments. Will this road become part of their limit to be set up there? What is the purpose of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
According to the information we have, and this has been checked with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, it is for the opening up of mining areas.
Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I hope there is something in that. I worked at Uchi Lake in 1939 before the mine closed down and I have had the impression since then, along with people who have lost money in the mines up there, that the prospects are not too good. In this particular case I am sure we thought the road would be of benefit to that particular pulp and paper company. This confirms the points the minister mentioned about discrimination. This road from Goldpines to Uchi Lake runs through what pulp and paper company's limit, and is the company involved in the deal in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We have not any information here concerning what pulp and paper company has crown lands in that area.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to know, in connection with this particular program, what the situation is so far as the road south from Hornepayne to hook up with the Ontario Paper Company's limits is concerned and which I believe is under the roads to resources program.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is not on
the roads to resources program. It may come under the forests access roads program.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It does not make sense that it would come under the forests access roads program in connection with the Ontario Paper Company because they already have limit roads up into that particular region. I cannot see why that road would be of any particular benefit to them, but it would be of benefit to the town of Hornepayne. I understood it was coming under this particular roads to resources program.
I should like an explanation of the road from Nakina northwest. What route has finally been decided upon? Is it the route that runs along the railroad track and then north, or is it going to be the original route that was bothering the people of Nakina?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It follows the railway track and then goes north.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not sure if the minister included this information in the beginning of his statement, but I should like to know whether the program includes a road from Foleyet to Chapleau?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, this was the second road on the program, Foleyet to Chapleau south approximately 60 miles. This work consists of new construction for the entire length commencing at the end of secondary highway No. 624 at Foleyet and
6178	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs proceeding in a southwesterly direction to connect with highway 129 in the vicinity of Chapleau.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the road to continue through Chapleau and will it hook up with the trans-Canada highway?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not under this agreement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The more I think of this question of these agreements with pulp and paper companies the more worried I become about the difficulties into which this government can get in that regard. I can think of so many paper companies throughout that area such as the Ontario Paper Company, Kimberly-Clark, St. Lawrence Corporation, Abitibi Power & Paper Co., Great Lakes Paper Co., Ontario-Minnesota Paper Co. and Dryden Paper Co. going from west to east, who all need forest road development. They would all have huge limits, and I suppose the average size is some fifteen hundred to two thousand square miles. Almost any of these companies could put forward a roads program that would be comparable to the Abitibi program. I can see the danger there.
I should like the minister to go into this in some detail with his provincial confreres because I can think of Marathon, especially, which still has not a road north from its mills into its limits. It has been working on a plan for a number of years and each year they plan to move a little bit further. However, I am sure that now with Abitibi getting this kind of program, which is in effect a high grade road, this kind of prospect must be very intriguing to a company like Marathon. I think it could, as I say, get the government into a great many problems in road construction. I would hope the minister would try to work out a fair policy in this regard and make sure that the provincial government has a fair policy so that no company is discriminated against in opening up its limits under this program.
There is another question I wanted to ask dealing with the two roads the minister mentioned north of the Canadian National. He said he could not give us the details but they were to open up various resources. One of the points that has bothered quite a number of foresters about that timber lying north of the Canadian National, especially the northwest corner near the Manitoba boundary, is the fact there is a budworm infestation that promises to increase considerably because of the state of maturity of the trees. Is this one of the regions in which this particular program is going? The minister knows the country well, and would the road take off 

from the O and M northern limit and go towards the Indian reservation along the Manitoba boundary?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We have no
knowledge where the road will start or where it will go. Actually the primary purpose of this road is to get at some promising mineral prospects that lie in a belt right up to the Manitoba boundary.
