maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could the minister tell us briefly what these legal difficulties are holding up these agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The first difficulty we ran into was what they called the time payment clause. This was proposed as a difficulty by Saskatchewan last November or December, if my memory serves me correctly. Then Saskatchewan proposed a new type of paragraph to cover this, and we finally agreed, as the federal government, to accept it. We said we would not accept it until we had spoken to all other provinces, and this led to a renegotiation of the time clause. When the time factor was changed, all the programs had to be re-examined and spread over the program, so that each province has a different amount planned for all the years of the program. This is not precise because in some provinces we have not fully concluded what the exact roads will be.
Then there is another legal difficulty about covenanting beyond the amount of $15 million if a road program costs more than $15 million. There is debate as to whether they should covenant themselves to complete the road when we do not know what the final cost will be. They were the same difficulties in the trans-Canada agreements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Can the minister explain why it was possible to conclude the agreement with British Columbia? Surely the same difficulty arose there as with the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This was done before I came into the department. As I understood it, it was a kind of quick deal on the part of the provincial and federal governments, and the province was not fully aware of what they had committed themselves to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think the minister has really let the cat out of the bag now. The one agreement which was concluded was concluded before this very experienced minister came into the department. It really is a very sorry chapter of fumbling and bumbling that we have been listening to all last Saturday and all this evening. All the time this minister has been in this department, with all his vast experience of domestic affairs, and in all those years he was losing elections in Saskatchewan when the Leader of the Opposition was sitting in the government of Canada helping to carry on the affairs of this country; during all that period when he was getting that experience, he was learning how to conclude agreements with his own province; secret agreements, agreements about matters so
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

secret that the public could not be told. I suggest to the minister, and I will not do anything more to hold up his estimates now, that he get rid of all this secrecy nonsense. If the minister had been able to get elected to any riding anywhere before 1957 he would have heard in this house, and probably joined in, the most terrific denunciation from his present leader about secrecy, orders in council, and things concealed from the public. Yet here this minister boasts day after day of how he is keeping things secret from parliament which are parliament's business. It seems to me that the sooner this ridiculous practice ends the better.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had something to do with this matter days ago and I am still a bit confused about what has happened. The minister did give some information, but I suggest to the minister that this information has been kicking around in various forms for some time. The hon. member for Timmins will tell you that the Chapleau-Foleyet road has been in the process of being built for many, many years; and also at the present time the minister of mines and forests in that area announces every week that another ten miles has been built. So there have been politics playing a part here, whether the minister knows it or not, and I suggest he has heard enough in this debate to realize that a great many of the problems would have been eliminated if he had brought in a report on the progress of these access roads. There is no secret about them. You may even find that some of the hon. members representing these areas know more than the minister's officials. Many of them have worked for the company involved and know considerable about them. I do not think there need be anything undercover about it. I think there needs to be a contract which will bind all parties with regard to these particular roads.
One of the minister's supporters the other day told me of his particular riding where this program is being used where they were fencing along the side of the road and they dug the fence posts the day before the provincial election, and the day after the election he informed me they went around and did not put posts in the holes but put the dirt back in, and that was the end of the program.
These things are happening. The minister can ask his backbenchers in the 26 seconds that each of them has in caucus, and they will tell him about these things. In any case, I suggest that he should set forth an account of how this money which we vote towards these roads is spent, in the same way as details of other projects are outlined

in the estimates. We should be told what progress is being made in the construction of these roads, where they are going, how they are being financed, and who is going to control them. I am very interested in these access roads. Many have been put in by the companies for fire protection and other reasons; they are fine, big, wide roads and there is often a gate on them. I recall in particular the road from Gowganda to Ramsey or to Sultan a few miles down the railway track. This road has been built for some time and is travelled by a number of people on permit. It could be made into a suitable highway, and I suggest this is one of the roads about which something could be done. But an agreement is going to be necessary or one of these days we will be told in this house that a road toward which federal grants have been contributed has a gate on it. The Abitibi company or the Marathon company will say it is not a public road and that the public has no right to travel over it. I suggest that some of these roads might with advantage be taken over by negotiation.
With regard to the other question, I do not think it is necessary to write a letter and take several weeks to consider these matters. I think these are decisions which would be made public at a time when tenders are called, as is the case with other jobs. We know of cases where roads have approached completion, yet the people in the area have never been informed where they are going or who is financing the project. I suggest the minister should take a lesson from this discussion which has, I believe, contained constructive criticism. The money which is spent by the federal government on this program gives us a complete right to know the details of these contracts, and I suggest that there must be contracts or we are not handling our finances in a satisfactory manner. If we give this money out in the form of grants, we should consider, say, $15 million to be a grant and give the money to a province to do with it what it likes. But as long as we are exercising some control we should give serious consideration to a better accounting system and to reaching a signed agreement in each case.
We in northern Ontario appreciate this program but we are losing a good deal of faith in it because we are always hearing some politician saying he has been given the latest word from the provincial parliament and the next road is going to be built for four miles in this or that direction to open up resources. I am sure that is not what the minister contemplated when he began to administer this program, and I say to
Supply-Northern Affairs him that it is within his power to end this type of speculation and give the people a much better understanding of the developments which are going to take place, and where the development roads are going to lead.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think I can bring up under this particular vote something that I think needs underlining because in my opinion it was one of the most regrettable bits of evidence that came before the committee looking into the affairs of the forestry branch. I refer to the evidence that this branch let some of its best silvicultural projects that had been in effect for some 30 years, and some of the best sample plots they had, go to the Department of National Defence because that department wanted a bit larger tank proving ground or manoeuvring ground for their troops. This to me is almost laughable when one considers the importance of silviculture in relation to the need of the army for an increased training ground. I know that national defence controlled this property at Petawawa and perhaps the forestry branch was there on sufferage.
I ask the minister this question. Why did he ever O.K. the wiping out of almost 50 per cent of the research areas for silviculture at Petawawa? Why did he not make some attempt to acquire that particular land on a permanent basis so these experimental areas could have been kept going? To me it was one of the most grievous blows silviculture has suffered. I understand that Major General Young was instrumental in bulling this through from the point of view of national defence. Someone bulled it through, anyway. To me it was a bad and stupid decision. I would like an


explanation as to why the forestry branch and the minister gave in so easily on this point.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I share and
appreciate the feelings of the hon. member concerning the loss of the silvicultural experimental areas at Petawawa. Every member of the forestry branch of my department would agree with me. The exigencies of the training program for national defence made it imperative for them to ask for this territory. I can assure the committee that the department has been reasonable with us. They are delaying the taking over of the property for defence purposes until we can get the maximum information available before the area is taken over.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: With sample plots it is not a question of 15 or 20 years to get results. You sometimes have to go through a whole cycle of up to 70 or 75 years. If there is any way the minister can salvage any of the regions that have been turned over I think he should give us his assurance that he will try to do so. When we consider that the Department of National Defence has that big camp at Gage-town and large areas at Camp Borden, and so on, to carry out manoeuvres, we fail to see any reason either in terms of economics or in terms of the defence needs of this country for the areas being allowed to go as a camp training ground or something of the kind. I do not think national defence is that important that in the light of the other areas national defence has silvicultural areas should be jettisoned. I hope the minister will try to save any of the plots that have not been already damaged by the military. In other words, I am suggesting to the minister that he try to renegotiate the matter if it is at all possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think the hon. member may have that assurance. First of all they have agreed to delay. Second, we are seeing what we can do to make the best of the situation. I think what the hon. member really wants is a statement of policy which I feel I can give him.
As far as the department is concerned we would like to have experimental areas entirely our own. As hon. members know the use of forest areas in the military reservations was just the start of the program but now that everybody accepts the task of the federal government in these vital research programs we do not want our programs hurt or interrupted by changes of policy on the part of the military who have a prior interest in the reservations. On this matter of forest products laboratories division, I should like to ask the minister whether any consideration is being given to helping small companies which are interested in establishing in those areas where the lumberng industry has been very hard hit? But there are other types of processes that are taking place, including the use of sawdust and shavings, and things of that nature, which could be advantageous to small companies if the research was done for them.
I know that some of this work has been done by the larger companies into such things as patent lumber, plywood, or bondwood-it is a kind of board, anyway, that is being manufactured by Abitibi at Sturgeon Falls. 

These programs take a great deal of money to develop. If some of the knowledge or information was available to much smaller companies they could probably go into production and thereby establish secondary industries.
I also think that some research should be done into handling the reforestation of a different kind of tree from what we are now growing. I am thinking of the United States where in the southern states they have developed a type of weed tree which, instead of taking 80 or 90 years to grow, as the white pine does, grows to a usable size in about 12 years. Some type of development along these lines would be very advantageous in northern Ontario and would help establish secondary industries.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I can answer very briefly the first part of the hon. gentleman's remarks about the helping of the small lumber operators. There is a great interest in the department in how we can shift our forest products research in helping the small operator. I have a few notes that I think would be of help to the committee.
The utilization of sawmill waste for the manufacture of wood pulp continues to show encouraging progress. Our laboratories continue to carry out research in barking, chipping and transportation of mill residues. Field studies of logging operations and of manufacturing plants include investigation into the effect of tree size on lumber manufacture, the influence of log defects on lumber quality, and the effect of prebarking on sawmill operations. Before we can speed up this help for the small operator we have to build up our research staff. This year we made a small start on what I look on as a five-year program. This year we put into the forest products research staff three additional professional officers and four technicians. I hope that by the end of about five years it will have the effect of doubling our efforts.
I would like to tell the committee about something else that has not been mentioned. What we are very proud of is a series of two-day courses on improved sawmilling techniques conducted by the Ottawa laboratories. This series was commenced last year and courses were given in April, 1959, at La Sarre, Quebec, and at Timmins, Ontario, each course being arranged in co-operation with the provincial department concerned and with the Canadian Lumbermen's Association. Further courses are to be given in British Columbia and in Saskatchewan this autumn. These courses have been attended by practical sawmill operators and have given rise to most favourable comments.

I could not say whether it should be dealt with by the forest products laboratory set-up or whether it should be a section that would be outside of that and work sort of generally in liaison with the Department of Trade and Commerce. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have had a number of letters and inquiries about this senior civil servant, the director of the archaeology branch, who has held this position for 10 years, I understand, and is still not a Canadian citizen. 293. To assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada, including grant of $5,000 to the Canadian tourist association, $2,319,342.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the minister care to comment on the activities of the bureau and its effect on this important Canadian industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Under its terms of reference the Canadian government travel bureau operates primarily to advertise Canada in the United States. Its purpose is to make as many Americans as possible conscious of the possibilities of Canada as a tourist spot and to draw them to this country. The bureau does not advertise in Canada. That is left to the provincial governments. There was a very thorough discussion of this matter in the standing committee, and I gave evidence there to the effect that I did think that selective advertising of the right sort, of a discriminatory sort to achieve the ends you wanted, would be wise. I said that in addition to advertising, some attention should be paid to what we call the tourist plant. In other words, there is very little use in advertising the beauty of an area if there are not facilities to handle the tourists going into that area.
We have tried to help out, as far as my department has been able to go so far, by the provision of the camp and picnic ground program which has been very successful. I think total expenditures amount to $6 million to date and in the next year or so expenditures will reach $10 million. The purpose of the program is to provide camp grounds and picnic sites along the highways of the provinces and the trans-Canada highway.


There are two separate types of agreements. There are many other things that have to be done.
This afternoon the house was discussing credit for small business. The tourist industry is largely a small business industry, and this is one of the things the government has been considering very seriously ever since the new government was formed. The problem has many complexities and one is the tourist business. The additional complexity affecting the department has to do with the national parks. The national parks do not give ownership of the land or property to a person building any type of plant and therefore it is very difficult for that person to get credit. There is a great need for credit in the tourist industry, which is mainly a small business industry. It is also an industry that we can use to attract many more people into Canada and equalize our balance of trade and develop the country. There is much to be done.
There is one other thing I have not mentioned. I have received a number of letters from various people across Canada saying that our forest access roads and roads to resources are being received with considerable satisfaction because tourists are very keen about finding their way into new areas. These roads are yielding revenues and benefits to the communities even before the forest areas or mineral resources are developed. I think that covers the activities of the travel bureau with the probable exception of the film activities which I think are well known.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Can the minister tell the house the volume of the tourist business to date this year compared to the same period last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is a little above last year, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could say what measures are being taken by the government through the travel bureau to offset the loss of business resulting from United States promotion urging their citizens to see their own country first, and what effect it has had?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The tourist business today is highly competitive. We have Europe, the West Indies, Mexico and even Asia now moving into competition in this tourist industry. Canada has to gear itself to meet this new competition because this is big business all over the world. Every year the dominion government and the provinces meet in a dominion-provincial conference. This year it will be in the latter part of November. In this meeting each of the eleven governments tries to lay down

a plan that will build up our operations, both at the provincial level and at the federal level. Both levels of government are always subject to the fact they have the fiscal conditions to meet.
I can assure hon. members that there is no activity between the federal government and the provinces in which I think there is more enthusiasm more awareness that much has to be done to help this tourist industry take advantage of the opportunities that are here and help meet this increasing competition.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I was asking what precisely is being done to offset this United States promotion this year; I am not talking about generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We have spent a little more money, not very much I know. We have a little more enticing advertising. We had openings in Chicago and New York of new offices and we are hoping to get enough money to get offices in the west coast of the United States, as well as other places.
Then again, we have been looking at the advertising and trying to get it into broader fields. Let me put it this way. One assumption we have been making in our advertising is that the people who are primarily interested are those who are close to Canada. I am not sure that is true. There is a large amount of evidence collecting that people who are getting information from away out in San Francisco are not interested in just going across the border, they are interested in the more distant parts. There has been a tremendous increase in long distance travel in both Canada and United States. We are trying to reach those United States citizens who are farther away from the Canadian border.
Then, some of us have the feeling that we could put on a special type of hot weather advertising in the southern states, advertising how cool it is in Canada while they are suffering from the heat.
